en: Preface to the *Qingzhu ji*:
Suppose one were to ask an ordinary person on the road, "Are Confucianism and Buddhism different? They would reply, "They are different. Yet Liu Zhi had a saying:
"The teachings of the Buddha advocate returning to the source by transcending attachments; this accords with the principle that life is originally quiescent, and thus does not contradict Confucius."
The Way of the Great Mirror (Bodhidharma) holds that the nature of beings is fundamentally good from beginning to end; that no weeding or tilling is required is taken as being in accord with Mencius.
Thus, the true expositions and secret truths of the Sage Gautama have, from the outset, been in harmony with the Confucian school.

His strictness in maintaining the person and his devotion to the Way are such that he might well be considered a Vinaya Master of the Confucian gate. As for the lineage of the "Flower-Picking and Smile," its influence has long since faded.
Alas! With every blow of the staff and every shout of "Ho," the essential meaning of Chan has become obscured. Consequently, people rely on words to establish written texts;
thus, the seventeen hundred public cases have been fashioned as mere regional analogies to be expounded to others. Their intent grows more diligent while the Dharma drifts further away.
Before long, the path of pure karma became faint, and external demons joined in their machinations—truly a period of "Yangjiu" calamity for the Empty Gate (Buddhism). —By Shi Zhi.
Zhao erected a banner at the shrine of pure vows and spent thirty years in summer retreat. Fellow practitioners, both monastics and laypeople, were encouraged to join in this collective endeavor.

In the intervals between their delight in Chan, they delved deeply into the inner scriptures. Compiling the works of various schools, they extracted and elucidated the meaning of the single transmission and secret entrustment, synthesizing them into a single volume.
Upon its completion, they sent a messenger on white-footed sandals to request a preface from me. I am but a follower of the Confucian tradition and am not [qualified].
Being well-versed in the terminology of the Śākya clan, how could one fail to perceive that which is sufficient to awaken both great and small practitioners?
One need only observe that its words are concise yet comprehensive, and its purport is refined yet vast;

without needing to possess a separate "hand-eye" (specialized insight), one already perceives the very marrow of the teaching. By following this path, one enters the inner sanctum; the lotus lamp points the way.
Having boarded the precious raft and reached the shore, he felt as if he were attending at the lion throne and listening to the sound of the ocean tide; was this not a cause for great joy?
Alas! As the Worthy Kalpa declined and the Elephant Teaching (Buddhism) fell into disuse, it had never been heard that anyone would open the locks and reveal such treasures as these, as did Ji-zhao.
Ji-zhao maintained a strict demeanor and possessed a profound faith in the Way; he devoted himself to the world of brush and ink.
Gathering the secrets not transmitted by the ancient virtuous ones, he desires to transform and deliver all sentient beings; thus, this mind is indeed noble yet weary.
Written by the Master of Qishu Lou, the Layman Venerable Zhao Chengxia, in the middle month of autumn in the Gengwu year.
Now, as for the "Clear Pearl," it is made of *borei* (crystal). When this pearl is cast into turbid water, the murkiness is entirely removed, and the bottom becomes clear.
It is clear and still. If it is placed in the mud, it wells up above the mire and stands out solitary and distinct.
Furthermore, although the substance of the pearl is extremely translucent, the myriad phenomena of the universe are neither reflected nor stained by it.

Only when the two pearls are held up against one another do their radiance intermingle, shining upon heaven and reflecting upon earth. The universal luminous wisdom of the Tathāgata Amitāyus is also like this. This...
When wisdom illuminates its locus, the afflictions of greed and anger melt away instantly like ice. Demons and heterodox paths are naturally subdued.
All that is passed through and all that remains are transformed into a single essence within the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm. Buddhas manifest one another;
the wisdom of universal radiance spans from antiquity to the present, eternally tranquil and eternally illuminating, without boundaries and without end. It is also like a great downpour of rain.
Dropping into the great ocean, they all become of one taste—the water of the sea. In the same way, the mindfulness of all sentient beings who recite the Buddha’s name is likewise so:
hundreds of thousands of millions of thoughts are all the True Suchness Dharma-realm, the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
Thus one knows that this Dharma-gate of Mindfulness of the Buddha is the supreme, sudden school; it is the sublime practice of directly transcending to enter the Buddha-wisdom. How joyful this is!
In this present life, let loyalty, filial piety, respect, and obedience be the foundation; let compassion and empathy be your primary practice.

At every moment and in every thought, illuminate these with the universal radiance of Amitābha’s wisdom; then there will be not a single thing that is not True Suchness (Tathatā), and not a single phenomenon that is not Buddha-wisdom.
Now, there are several dozen lay practitioners who, sharing a common vow, have resolved their minds to form a society for the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Herein [they shall...]

The *Qingzhu ji* (Collection of Pure Mantras), compiled by the Venerable Huankong, has been carved for printing and widely disseminated, with the desire that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm may together perfect the All-Knowing Wisdom (*sarvajñā*).
This may truly be called a lotus blooming from the mud; dwelling amidst the dust yet transcending it, it is most rare indeed.

If one can maintain pure mindfulness in succession, with a single mind undisturbed, focusing the thought until it becomes still, so that both subject and object are forgotten, then one will ultimately realize this very mindfulness.
Directly entering the ocean of the true suchness of Amitābha’s dharma-nature, they travel together through the Flower Treasury lands of Vairocana.
Until the end of the future, they shall deliver and liberate sentient beings in measureless and boundless numbers; for this reason, I rejoice and am delighted to compose this preface.
On the Day of the Dragon-Boat Festival in the year of Dunchang (the Year of the Sheep), I, Dezhen of the Vow-Staff Mountain Man, Xuzhou Hall,
respectfully bow and write this preface.
The Sūtra says: A person has a wish-fulfilling jewel tied to his own garment, yet he is unaware of it.

Wandering in poverty and exposure in a foreign land, he suddenly encounters a wise man who points out the jewel to him. His every wish is then fulfilled according to his heart, bringing about great abundance.

Only then does he realize that the divine jewel was not obtained from without. Thus one knows that within the sphere of each and every person, there is a priceless precious jewel—luminous, translucent, and pure.
It is transparent and constantly emits great radiance. Thus, an ancient verse says: "The wondrous *prajñā*-pearl is difficult to fathom;
within the ocean of *dharmatā*, it is personally recognized. This pearl is neither large nor small; its radiance illuminates all day and night. This is precisely what that refers to.

As for the dragon girl offering her pearl and receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), it is the pearl of the pearl-less. As for the *wangxiang* seeking the pearl, it is the attainment of the mindless.
To mistake fish eyes for pearls is to mistake a thief for one’s own son; to buy the casket and return the pearl is to lose the truth through delusion.
Furthermore, there are *maṇi* jewels, Indra’s net jewels, crest-jewels, and jewels held in the palm—these various kinds of jewels are none other than the manifestation of this very jewel of the mind.
Thus, Yongjia understood the pearl, Danxia admired the pearl, Guannan obtained the pearl, and Shaoshan refined it.
The ancients were truly justified in their earnest pursuit of this "pure pearl" (qingzhu).
I am currently compiling essential passages on the Pure Land from various masters, titling it *The Collection Named the Pure Pearl*.

This is intended to capture the meaning of how a pure pearl cast into turbid water cannot fail to purify it, and how mindfulness applied to a distracted mind cannot fail to unify it. —The Society for Pure Vows.

My friend wished to entrust this to the carver to broaden the fellowship among like-minded companions, and thus established these regulations for our community. I have provided this "Verification of the Pearl" as a preface to the volume.

Alas! Since we have already reached the place of treasure, we must surely seek out the pearl from the black dragon and grasp the numinous serpent; how could we possibly return empty-handed with nothing?
If one can recognize that the pearl is inherently present within the lining of this robe, then one will certainly have no leisure to concern oneself with others.
Counting the jewels, what else could there be in this collection? Yet, in the end, where exactly are those pearls? Alas!
The moon in the empty expanse over the azure depths of ten thousand ages—only after searching and dredging again and again will you finally know it.
On the day of the Buddha’s Bathing Festival in the intercalary month of the ninth year of the Tongzhi era, the year of Gengwu (1870),
the śramaṇa Hwankong of Seogyak Mountain recorded these prefaces at Leoxiguan in Puguang Temple.

Books concerning the Pure Land are so numerous that they exhaust oxen carrying them and fill the rafters of houses. This collection, however, excerpts from various masters, eliminating all redundancy and superfluity.
Like sifting through sand to find gold, it aims to awaken practitioners with even a single phrase or half-verse;
furthermore, I have not dared to arbitrarily insert my own opinions.
In each case, I have not recorded who said that a certain book was produced [by a specific person]. This is like gathering furs to make a robe;
the value lies in having no visible seams, so as to form a unified body of discourse. My intention is merely to inspire faith in readers and encourage their diligent practice.
Furthermore, I have fully listed the sources from which these citations were drawn; those of broad learning and refined character should naturally understand their origins through silent reflection.

There are two gates for the skillful means of rebirth in the Pure Land: first, visualization; second, the recitation of the name. This collection is dedicated exclusively to the practice of reciting the name while omitting visualization.

This is because the minds of sentient beings are coarse and visualization is difficult to accomplish. Furthermore, in this land, those with the capacity for practice find that reciting the name is extremely easy;
thus, if one has a sincere vow, one will certainly be reborn there.
I have excerpted and selected from various masters, much like assembling experienced and effective prescriptions from many physicians.
Although there is some repetition and a lack of systematic order, my primary aim is the awakening of oneself and others; thus, it is not improper to offer these instructions repeatedly.
This work exclusively expounds upon the Pure Land while simplifying the Chan school. It is based on the principle that "if one has Chan but lacks Pure Land, nine out of ten will err;
whereas if one has Pure Land but lacks Chan, ten out of ten will attain liberation. Yet, although the expedient means are manifold, the return to the source is non-dual;

how then could Chan and Pure Land ever diverge? Only when one reaches the source through both investigation and recitation will one realize that there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference between them.

This collection is not divided into categories; it contains sections on exhortation, inspiring faith, practice, making vows, preparing for the end, meritorious deeds, upholding the precepts, encouraging filial piety, correct discernment, and citing parables.
It begins with the Buddha within oneself and concludes with the realization that there is nothing that is not the Buddha.
This is intended to enable the reader to suddenly awaken to the Buddha of one’s own nature and immediately realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Reflecting upon my own meager learning and limited scope, my research has not been exhaustive; thus, the few rules I have compiled cannot avoid omitting ten thousand others.
Should these be supplemented as they are encountered, I leave them for the sake of future worthies within our scholarly community.
Cited sources include:
*The Treatise on the Ten Doubts Concerning the Pure Land* (Zhiyi); *The Jewel King Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation* (Fei Xi);
*The Treatise on Rebirth* (Dao’an); and *The Treatise on Resolving Various Doubts* (Huai Gan).
*Anle ji* (Dàocháo); *Jingtu cibei ji* (Címǐn); *Wànshàn tóngguī ji* (Yǒngmíng); *Wǎngshēng jìngtù chānyuàn yí* (Cíyún);
*Zhǐzhí jìngtù juéyí jí* (Wáng Gǔ); *Bǎozhū jí* (same author).
*Longshu Jingtuwen* (Wang Xuzhong); *Guiyuan Zhizhiji* (Zongben);
*Jingtu Hewen* (Tianru); *Sanshi Xini Yanfan* (Mingben); *Jingtu Lijiao Zhi* (Zhipan); *Jizhaoji*.
*The White Lotus Collection* (Lianzong baojian), by Pudu;
*The Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha Collection* (Nianfo zhizhi ji), by Miaoye; *The Mirror of Mindfulness of the Buddha* (Nianfo jing), by Daojing;
*The Dharma Compendium of Yunqi* (Yunqi fahui), by Zhuhong; and *The Collection on the Return to the Pure Land* (Jingtu zhigui ji), by Dayou.
*Ci'en Tongzan* (Kuiji), *Xifang Helun* (Yuan Hongdao),
*Lebang Wenlei* (Zongxiao), *Jingtu Chenzhong* (Zhou Kerufu),
*Guxiang Xiaoxi* (Ding Mingdeng), *Lianlou Qingyin* (Lotus Companions).
*Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land* (Wang Tian);
*Repentance Method for the Chan-Nian Amitābha Practice Hall* (Wang Zicheng); *Book on the Lotus World* (Tang Yizhi);
*Pure Land Dharma Words* (Wujin); *Collection from Dream Journeys* (Deqing).
*Jingxintang ji* (Zhi Xu); *Jingtu sheng wusheng lun* (Chuan Deng);
*Foding zhu* (Shi Chengjin); *Xifang gongju* (Qing Lian). Table of Contents.
Directly accepting the Buddha’s secret Dharma-gate within oneself—profound yet simple;
the six perfections and myriad practices as the true cause of the One Vehicle; the correct view of ultimate emptiness—attain it immediately upon seeking.
Whether noble or base, a single stumble leads to a hundred stumbles in a drunken dream.
In my daily life, whether upright or horizontal, I seek a place of rest;
yet I know that nature and temperament are suffering, and that liberation from suffering lies in transformation.
This deluded person follows karma as a "fine fellow" born within his own mind; in reality, there is no coming or going, nor are there any ranks or stages.
Great Virtue, great merit, and the dharma-body as retribution for past deeds—this single case is like autumn grass and winter cicadas;
unattached, it is as if a fleeting dream. Beware of being entangled by others;
exchange the small for the great, examine this precarious body with care, and exert yourself!
Warning the aged: you must cast away the illness of attachment to precepts;
this is not a matter of my own joy or sorrow, gain or loss, for nothing can be taken with you.
Resolve your will with the firmness of linked chains, set aside all worldly affairs, and practice the Dharma early, for impermanence is intimately related to our very nature.

Regarding the ten kinds of faith as Mount Sumeru, the third is the faith of dedication through concentration, which must certainly be attained by now. One should contemplate deeply and believe with earnest conviction that even crawling insects can be brought to peace and made into subjects;
yet, being constrained by one's own limited views, one fails to see their efficacy, deceiving oneself and abandoning them with arrogance.
Among all dharmas of merit, this alone is the King; in a single thought-moment, one gains mastery over the very life-root of oneself.
When the true realm is revealed and the names "Zhang San" and "Li Si" are cast aside, they naturally become a single expanse. Moving toward this density, one awakens.
Truly mindful of the initial aspiration, let it surge like billowing waves;
with murmuring reverence, the five respects fully gather the six sense faculties. Set a fixed period for accomplishment, practicing in stillness and refining through movement;
cultivate with single-minded devotion morning and evening, reciting the ten recollections as your daily practice.
When the mind and breath rely upon each other, one should contemplate rebirth;

through focused study and contemplation, the flower of the mind will directly and simply blossom. Through the refined clarity of the Samādhi of One Appearance, by visualizing the white curl between the Buddha’s brows, one shall behold various auspicious signs.
The fool cannot exert effort; at the very first step of authentic practice, one must not allow for negligence.
Third, when the three conditions are precisely met, the hundred artisans and the four classes of people act with rectitude.
One should maintain a secret recollection of the bodhicitta—the three minds.
May the rain of liberation drench my head; may I be forever steadfast, one-pointed in mind, and single-minded.
May all that is heard and seen transform anger into joy. May this raft carry me across the river to the ultimate stillness.
O King of Vows, enter directly into the unconditioned; may this verse of dedication fulfill all aspirations.
Through the meeting of like natures with the Vajra Banner of Sincerity, one will surely receive guidance;
having reached the place of birth, there shall never again be regression. For a thousand years, the news of harmony is received;
when the mind is devoid of substance, all that accords with one's wishes is fully manifested. Ring the chime!
The Equalizing Guide-Car returns to its native land; auspicious responses are manifold.
This talisman protects the body: of the three doubts and four barriers, one attains seven parts.
Do not harbor thoughts of prior cultivation when the thief has fled and the gate is closed; it is like the time it takes to milk a cow.
Comparing suffering and pleasure, there is nothing but goodness; taking this as a test, one stays far from Māra.
The seven excellences: reciting with a loud voice, exhorting others to cultivate merit, and paying homage to the Buddha.
The ten losses incurred by not cultivating [merit], and the ten kinds of merit [of cultivation]. The ten excellences of the Pure Land and the ten easeful ways of rebirth.
The pure garland of all precepts is like a jewel that awakens one to the fact that emotions,
enemies, and kin are as remote and dark as the void; the seventh is the precept against releasing living beings and killing,
for the nature of form and its causes are eternally as they are— though a single thread may bind them, it is essential to cut off the root and the trunk.
Supramundane filial piety assists one's parents in their journey to the West to repay their kindness;
it universally delivers all beings through mutual support in virtuous practice, remaining free from any flaw or blemish.
Through the "Ten Minds" and the "Fourfold Examination," one should fully prepare to study this Dharma, weighing it against the analogy of the three-stranded rope.

Having left the household life, the King of Physicians, Mātharīputra, employs the six sense faculties in their objects to eliminate the mind of self-attachment. When the principle of emptiness is realized and the mind is stilled, the nature of phenomena manifests;
the nature of karma being empty, even ten thousand oxen cannot pull him back as he maintains his resolve in solitude.
Carefree and joyful, one nurtures life while forgetting death; yet the five delusions willingly lead one into mire and fire.
With false views and arrogance, the *agada* medicine for preventing death is wasted on so many examples.
Laughter and weeping alternate; it is difficult for even a small amount of goodness to arise—like sealing wax pressing into clay.
The hundred-jin gold verifies the two sufferings of birth and death;

the ten difficulties concern the flight and fall of emotional thoughts. Good causes lead to evil fruits; when one attains the meaning, one forgets the words. Regarding the gain and loss of the physical form, there are two types of heavenly beings;
small causes and effects provide the necessities for life and assist the Way, resulting in no suffering.
The Unobstructed Interpenetration of Quiescence and Function; The Falsehood Departed is the Reality;
There is Nothing in Delusion or Enlightenment that is Not Buddha (Appendix: Society Charter, Vow Text, Fund-Raising Appeal, Precept Repentance Text, *Qingzhu ji*).
Compiled by Shi Huan Kongtang Zhizhao, Master of the Jingyuan Society at Puguang Temple on Mount Guling:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time are all entirely within one's own body; yet, because they are obscured by habitual tendencies and turned by external objects and conditions,"
One is deluded by oneself. If there is no mind within the mind, that is the Buddha of the past. To be tranquil and unmoving is the Buddha of the future.
To respond to things according to their conditions is the Buddha of the present. To be pure and untainted is the Buddha free from defilement.
To be unimpeded in coming and going is the Buddha of Supernatural Powers; to roam freely everywhere is the Buddha of Sovereign Freedom;
for the single mind to remain unclouded is the Buddha of Radiance; for the aspiration for the Way to be firm and steadfast is the Indestructible Buddha; and for great compassion to be vast—
This is precisely Amitābha Buddha. Yet nowadays, when people see the Buddhas of the ten directions, they regard them as something extraordinary and marvelous, while regarding themselves as inferior.

They do not realize that the Buddhas are merely ordinary people acting according to their true nature, and that ordinary people are merely Buddhas who have failed to act according to their true nature.
They cast aside the precious treasure within their own lot, yet willingly endure hardships beyond their station.
I take full responsibility for this myself; it is truly pitiable and lamentable.

Regarding the secret Dharma-gate, the ancients taught that one should draw near to an enlightened teacher and seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, such a spiritual friend truly possesses nothing to transmit through words or mind.
The bestowing of the secret dharma-gate consists solely in untying the person's adhesions and removing their fetters; this is precisely what is meant by "secret.
Now, simply upholding the name with single-mindedness and without distraction—these eight characters are themselves the secret dharma-gate for untying adhesions and removing fetters.
Do not seek anything else further.
Directly take up the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates; they are all not equal to a single phrase of the Buddha. Even the seventeen hundred public cases are likewise not [equal].
It is like the single phrase "Buddha. Why is this? Because this one gate alone possesses both the sudden and the gradual, as well as the principle and the traces.

Those of superior faculties and wisdom directly accept it and, realizing their nature, attain Buddhahood. As for those of middling or inferior capacities who cannot yet transcend suddenly, they rely on the power of that Buddha and all attain rebirth there. Thus, this gate surpasses all others.
Profound, subtle, simple, and easy:
this Way is most profound and most subtle, and likewise most simple and most easy. Because it is so simple and easy, those of lofty intelligence overlook it.
Indeed, birth and death do not depart from a single thought-moment; even all the myriad dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds do not depart from this one.
Contemplate: Right now, use this very mindfulness to recite the Buddha’s name. What could be more immediate, proximate, essential, and substantial?
If you can penetrate to the source from which this mindfulness arises, that is the Amitābha of one's own nature; it is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.

By the power of this mindfulness, one will be reborn in the Pure Land, thereby cutting across birth and death horizontally and no longer undergoing saṃsāra; one will immediately realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The six perfections and myriad practices are encompassed within a single phrase of the Buddha; the eight teachings are fully subsumed within the Perfect [Teaching]. It is the ultimate doctrine and principle of the three baskets and twelve divisions of the canon;
it is the upward-moving pivot of the seventeen hundred public cases; it is the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle conducts; it is the three clusters of pure precepts.
All precepts are contained therein. To be truly able to practice the Buddha-remembrance and to let go of the world of body and mind is itself great generosity (*dāna*).
No longer giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion is itself great ethical discipline (*śīla*). Not calculating self versus others or right versus wrong is itself great patience (*kṣānti*).
Not allowing even the slightest interruption or admixture of other thoughts is itself great diligence (*vīrya*). Not being deluded by divergent paths is itself great wisdom (*prajñā*). Not...
Furthermore, those who, amidst the pursuit of deluded thoughts, enter the great meditative concentration (mahā-dhyāna) as practitioners of the single vehicle’s correct cause—
namely, those who practice Buddha-recollection— seek only the fruit of Buddhahood of the single vehicle as their goal, and harbor no false hopes for other vehicles. Thus they resolve their minds.

To cultivate the Pure Land with such a mind is called the true cause. If it were otherwise, then even if one were diligent in recollecting the Buddha, because the causal ground would not be true, the resulting fruit would be circuitous.
The past is empty before the present void; the present is empty before one's eyes; the future is definitively empty.

All worldly conditions—whether pleasant, like clusters of brilliant colored clouds, or unpleasant, like turbid mist obscuring the sky—are thus. Yet, when people encounter circumstances that accord with their own desires, they give rise to...
Attachment arises when things are pleasing; aversion arises when they are disagreeable. This merely increases black karma (unwholesome deeds). Where, then, is the true reality?
One must constantly contemplate all things through the lens of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and not cling to them as being existent, for such clinging only obstructs one's own mind. As the Sūtra says:

"There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span. This is what is called the *prajñā* of true emptiness—the foremost and most urgent teaching for transcending the world.
This is indeed so.

For one who cultivates pure karma with right knowledge and vision and aspires to birth in a Pure Land, although this is attained through the refinement of practice, if one does not encounter right knowledge and vision—
When people preach the Dharma to guide others, if they do not grasp its essential principles, they may fall into error and inverted views, practicing along mistaken paths;
thus, one must be diligent. It is like a farmer tilling his fields: though he exerts great effort, the growth remains sparse until the timely rains descend, whereupon flowers and fruits flourish.
When the wheels and wings move together, and the eyes and feet provide mutual support, one avoids the misfortunes of blindness and lameness. Great!

Among the monastics and laypeople who recite the Buddha’s name, many do not understand the underlying principle. They may be subjected to groundless derision and slander by those who cling to the view of emptiness, which gives rise to doubt in their hearts and ultimately leads to their regression and loss. This is because they have not heard the Dharma.
That which is sought is immediately obtained;
though the external body is seen, it is originally non-existent, like a bubble upon the water that suddenly arises and then vanishes.
The internal body is not seen, yet it is originally existent, like fire within wood that is obtained as soon as one seeks it. Those who study these [truths] clearly should understand this.
It remains thus. Not knowing the fire within the wood, how can one seek it? With single-minded right mindfulness, whether noble or base, if one thinks, "This is gold and jade;
this is gravel and stone," then even a child of three feet in height would surely discard the stone.
When seeking gold, one takes it spontaneously without being exhorted, precisely because one recognizes its value. It is the same for the practitioner:
having clearly recognized that this land is suffering while that land is bliss, and that this is the drowning of birth and death while that is sovereign liberation.
One must also necessarily abandon defilement to seek purity. Naturally, from moment to moment there is no abiding; mind after mind is unceasing, like one whose head is on fire.
Upon hearing the teaching, one acts immediately;
even a single lapse is a hundred lapses.
The ancients said: "If one does not practice in this life, one miss is a hundred misses. From one to a hundred—how many misses there are! It reaches this very point. As the sutras state:
"It is difficult to leave the evil realms and obtain a human body; it is difficult to obtain a human body and encounter the Buddha-dharma;
yet, to encounter the Dharma-door of Buddha-remembrance and accept it with faith is even more difficult. As the sutras describe, the ants themselves...

Since the time of the Seven Buddhas, they have not yet escaped their ant-bodies; how can one know on what day they will obtain a human body, on what day they will encounter the Buddha-dharma, or on what day they will encounter the Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha and receive it with faith? It is not merely a hundred missed opportunities;
indeed, there are a thousand and ten thousand missed opportunities, endless in number. How tragic!

The world of the intoxicated and dreaming is roughly divided into two types: the wealthy and noble, and the poor and lowly. Those who are poor and lowly are certainly busy from morning until night, laboring to provide food and clothing.
Those who are wealthy and noble are likewise busy from morning until night, striving to enjoy sensual pleasures. While their modes of enjoyment differ, their busyness is the same.
First: one is busy until death, yet the mind does not cease its toil. Carrying this mind with one into the next life, one is born again, busies oneself again, and dies again.
Through this cycle of birth and death, birth and death, one remains dark and obscured, as if intoxicated or dreaming, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas without ever reaching an end.
Only by being born in the Pure Land can one awaken clearly and alone.

To make a living plan based on this body is to treat a mere inert corpse as one’s livelihood. That which is vibrant and pulsing within it is the living being. Do not make your living plan out of the dead thing;
you should make your living plan out of the living being. All those who covet external objects and offer up all manner of things [to them]—

The physical body is merely making a living upon that which is already dead. Although worldly people have not yet been able to escape this, they ought to carve out a brief moment of leisure amidst their worldly pursuits and bodily maintenance to turn the light inward and reflect upon themselves, thereby fixing their minds on the Pure Land;
this is making a living upon that which is truly alive.

Practicing the Way through other gates in a vertical manner is called "vertical transcendence of the triple world. Reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land is called "horizontal transcendence of the triple world.

It is like a worm inside a bamboo stalk: if it moves vertically, it is difficult to pass through the nodes; if it moves horizontally, it penetrates all at once. This is the most direct and expedient method. It is the most...

How extraordinary! Therefore it is said: "In the ocean of birth and death, the recitation of the Buddha's name is supreme. To live a hundred years without hearing these words is worse than being a child who has heard them. To have read ten thousand scrolls of books without hearing these words is worse than being a fool who has heard them. Now that you have heard them, there is still the matter of faith or lack thereof; and even if you have faith, there is the matter of practicing or not practicing. Thus it is said: [The text continues with verses: "Even if one lives for a hundred years, If one does not hear this teaching, It is better to be a child who hears it. Even if one reads ten thousand scrolls, If one does not hear this teaching, It is better to be a fool who hears it. Therefore, it is only those beings of great resolve who are uniquely able to rouse themselves and bring an end to birth and death.
Seeking a place to settle down is like a person entering a great city who must first find a place to stay before going out to attend to business;
thus, when evening falls and it grows dark, there will be a place to lodge. Seeking a place to settle down first refers to the cultivation of the Pure Land. When evening arrives—

"The evening turning to pitch black" refers to the arrival of one's great destiny (death). "Having a place to lodge for the night" refers to being reborn within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms.
Sentient emotion is *qing* (feeling); spiritual lucidity is *xing* (nature). Spiritual lucidity can give rise to knowledge; knowledge can delude spiritual lucidity.
Ordinary people all allow knowledge to delude their spiritual lucidity; therefore, they follow knowledge in being born and dying again and again. If...

If one can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, such that all conditioned knowledge is exhausted and the void becomes transparent and penetrating, sharing the same essence as the Great Void, one will naturally transcend birth and death.
This is itself non-arising; this is itself the Pure Land; this is itself Sukhāvatī.

Knowing suffering and desiring to emerge from it, one wishes to enter this gate. First, one must know suffering. Once suffering is known, one must seek its cessation. All sentient beings take suffering to be pleasure;
they do not reflect that this body has, since immeasurable kalpas past, only briefly resided among humans and devas, its appearance as fleeting as a flash of lightning.
Suddenly, one may find oneself amidst copper pillars and iron beds, the soul wandering through the hells; or suddenly, among beasts and birds, one’s blood stains the butcher’s block and blade.
All this is due to being dragged by the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*), revolving endlessly like an ox pulling a millstone.

Having now temporarily obtained this human body, aging, decline, sickness, and death are more rapid than the act of breathing. Impure secretions are no different from a stinking corpse. If one does not awaken—
With a resolute mind, one gives rise to the practice of diligence. By what means does one attain liberation?

Through the transformation [of perception], one realizes that my Buddha-body is profound, eternally quiescent, and devoid of coming or going. The consciousness-mind of sentient beings relies upon the merit of the Buddha’s original vows.
O Śrībalin, the transformations of one’s own mind involve coming and going; know that when pure karma has matured, one beholds the Buddha-body for oneself.

When evil retribution is about to be realized, the mind manifests as hell. It is like a person of superior merit who grasps pebbles and turns them into gold, while a person poor in karma transforms gold into pebbles.
This transformation is "I"; what concern have the gold and the pebbles?
Deluded people recite the Buddha’s name without sincerity; they merely regard the two words "birth and death" with indifference throughout their lives.
Busily preoccupied, they cast their very lives into the void as if it had no connection to themselves at all. Even when...
The scene: sighing for but a moment, one’s hair stands on end and one’s bones tremble. Yet after this, one returns to the same state of drunken dream. Tu Chuihe said:
"Worldly wisdom is in disarray within the field of fame and profit; the clever consciousness-spirit is in turmoil upon the road of birth and death. How lamentable!

Who understands that the four elements are not solid, that impermanence is exceedingly swift, and that the three paths and eight difficulties are most bitter and extreme in their suffering? Who would—"
What is essential is to recite the Buddha’s name with earnest sincerity; such people are but one or two in a hundred.
