He then concealed it and refused to speak of it. How utterly deluded he was! For it is because the spirit comes and takes refuge in this form that we call it "life";
because the spirit departs and leaves this form that we call it "death. Thus, the spirit is the self, while the form is the dwelling of the self.
Since the self has coming and going, its dwelling undergoes formation and decay. Furthermore, from whence does the spirit come?
They come according to the conditions of karma; how could the spirit depart of its own accord? It departs according to the conditions of karma.
Since beginningless time, it has entered wombs and changed shells, unable to remain long in a single place. This is because the karma we have created does not endure for long.
As for that which does not perish: the spirit dwells within karma. When karma is exhausted, the form perishes;

when the form perishes, the spirit has no place to dwell, and it departs according to the karma created by oneself in this present life. Thus, how could the place to which one goes not be anticipated?
It is like a person who builds a house and must surely reside in it, or prepares a feast and then partakes of it; therefore, one acts in this manner.
Karma must inevitably bring such retribution; if one cultivates pure karma in the present life, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain—what further cause for doubt could there be?
Even those considered "fine men" who are renowned throughout the world are themselves merely fine men among a thousand or ten thousand people. Yet, even so...
Yet we all take this world to be our own permanent abode where we shall never depart.
To one with clear vision, every form is but a passing shadow; in the blink of an eye, so much has already vanished.
It is just like puppets on a stage, momentarily laughing and playing, until their creator pulls the strings and hangs them upon the top of a wall pillar. Alas!
Within this enclosure of wood, there is a space of one foot five inches square; could this possibly be the place where you dwell?
If you can make a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land, to abide in the stage of non-retrogression, and to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, only then may you be called a true hero.
Born from within one's own mind:
the empty space of the ten directions is immeasurable and boundless, and the measure of the mind can encompass all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
My own mind, immeasurable and countless, pervades each and every one of them. Viewed in this light, the hundred trillion lands are within my own mind.
In reality, it is extremely near; how could there be any distance? At the moment of death and rebirth, the birth occurs within one's own mind;

in reality, it is extremely easy; how could there be any difficulty? Provided that sentient beings have perfected the karma for the Pure Land, the concentrated mind at the end of life is itself the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land. If one stirs a thought, in the mere twinkling of an eye, one attains rebirth.

In reality, there is no coming or going for the Great Vow-holding Sages; though they come from the Pure Land, their coming is truly no-coming. For ordinary beings with deep resolve, they go to the Pure Land, yet their going is truly no-going.
Those sages do not come here, nor do these beings go there, yet the sages and ordinary beings meet, and both attain [their goal].
What is meant by "interacting"? The light of Amitābha is like the pure, full moon, shining universally throughout the ten directions.
When the water is clear and still, the moon appears in its entirety; yet the moon does not suddenly come there to take up the water.

When the water is turbid and moving, the moon lacks a fixed radiance; yet the moon does not suddenly depart, abandoning the water. Thus, while the water possesses clarity or turbidity, stillness or motion, these qualities do not exist within the moon itself.
In the taking and discarding, the coming and going, there are no stages;

in a single thought-moment of diligence, karma is transformed into cause. In a single thought-moment of retreat or deficiency, conditions are transformed into karma. From a pit of fire, it becomes a lotus throne.
In the mere instant of a single thought-moment, Amitābha Buddha is ever with the sentient beings of the six realms; there are stages of attainment, yet no hierarchical distinctions,
for they possess great virtue and great merit.
People today look down upon the Western Pure Land and are unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is because they do not realize that rebirth in the West is the path of those with great virtue, great merit, great wisdom, and great sagehood;
it is a matter of transforming this Sahā world into a pure land, which is no ordinary cause or condition. You need only observe this city: how many people die within a single day and night? Do not...
To say that one who is reborn in the Western Land is immediately reborn in heaven is to claim that not even one in a thousand or ten thousand people achieves this.
Those who pride themselves on their practice do no more than avoid losing their human form.
Repaying past retributions within the burning house of the three realms, one receives a body bound by karma; whether the lifespan is long or short, it is entirely a repayment of past retributions.

If in a previous life there was a ten-year allotment, one experiences those ten years in this life; if in a previous life there was a twenty-year allotment, one experiences those twenty [years] in this life.
Ten years pass. Of those who live a hundred years, those who reach seventy are rare. When the great limit arrives, one must return to death.
Consider, for instance, those families of fame, office, and wealth: their treasures are like mountains and their wives and concubines fill the rooms;
they rejoice day and night. How could they not wish to live long in this world? Yet alas, their future is finite; it is driven on in secret. When the tally arrives, it must be executed.
The Old Man Yama does not follow human sentiment; what face would the King of Impermanence have?
Moreover, it is witnessed directly by everyone’s own eyes and heard directly by their own ears throughout the streets and alleys: relatives and kin, friends and brothers.
Though one may be strong and young, how many have already died? An ancient said: "Do not wait until old age before you study the Way;
the solitary graves are all those of the young."
Ordinary people do not know that the Dharma-body is their own fundamental nature; instead, they mistake this provisional body composed of the four elements for True Suchness.
They fail to recognize the hundreds of thousands of clear waters of the great ocean, yet they mistake a single floating bubble or foam upon the sea for the ocean itself.
Thereupon, relying upon this provisional body, one commits various karmic offenses. One seeks high and spacious palaces to house this body;
one seeks fine silks and brocades for clothing to adorn this body; one seeks rare and exquisite food and drink to satiate this body;
one seeks light and sturdy carriages and horses to ease this body; one seeks beautiful sounds and sights to delight this body. Thus, there arises the notion of "self" and "others."
From this, distinctions arise; greed, stinginess, anger, joy, right and wrong, and honor and disgrace are born. Infinite karmic offenses of a single lifetime all originate from this.
One day, when these four elements undergo transformation and decay, they all return to nothingness, yet it is the conscious spirit that must bear the karmic retribution.
To remain thus deluded and fail to awaken is to suffer the cycle of rebirth in vain; this is truly pitiable. If one can awaken to this as...
The provisional is merely a temporary lodging; one lives out a hundred years in a coarse manner, seeking nothing to please the mind and committing no transgressions for the sake of others.
Once the provisional is realized, the real manifests before one: mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely revealed as the Dharmakāya, and one no longer clings to floating bubbles.
One then beholds the great ocean. Knowing this, one further understands that the Pure Land must be cultivated.
Throughout one's life—from youth to maturity, and until old age and the brink of death—if one does not know how to plan for it, it is either because of delusion and forgetfulness, or because of fear.
It is merely that people avoid speaking of it. Furthermore, when people fear death, they do not truly fear it.

When one suddenly comes into being, grows in a state of dull ignorance, and finally declines into old age and death—through these flickering and transient moments—one is incessantly submerged in the river of affection and the sea of desire;
one is incessantly dragged by the tether of fame and the shackles of profit. Then, in a single morning, all turns to ash.
The cold fire passes on as the wood is replaced; at the final move of this game, who can escape?
From this point forward, extinguishing and then being born again, the three realms and six paths revolve like a waterwheel. To examine one's own conduct, one seeks death and rebirth day after day;
to fail to seek liberation from the karma of birth and death—this may truly be called "pitying oneself yet not fearing death. If one were truly able to...
Fearing death, one must surely seek liberation; yet if one abandons the recollection of the Buddha, what path shall one follow? If one abandons the Pure Land, with whom shall I return?
Autumn grasses and winter cicadas.
Looking only at what lies before us, cold and heat urge us on; how is this different from flowing waves or flashing lightning?
When we turn our heads to forty or fifty years ago, people and things have suddenly melted away. Who among those who experienced the bitterness and joy of that time did not cling to them in delusion?

Yet now, the autumn grasses and winter cicadas—their forms and sounds—have both transformed, giving way to an entirely new scene that they no longer perceive. Those who look back at the present will see it as we do now.
How tragic! Those who are deluded act with reckless haste; those who have attained awakening procrastinate. In this state of restless turmoil and frantic busyness, what is truly real?
There is only the single path of the life-force (*jīvitendriya*) that can lead one to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*); it is so that this flame in the wind may not go to waste.
An ancient teaching says: "This day has passed, and life is likewise diminished. It further says: "Today, too, has thus been spent in vain. Has it not?
Knowing what tomorrow may bring, upon hearing these poignant words, how could one’s heart not tremble and the hair on one's body stand on end?
To be greedily attached to useless and empty affairs, wasting away one's limited lifespan—reflecting on the past and pursuing the future, this is truly lamentable and pitiable.
Fields, gardens, houses, gold, silver, wealth, and silks—none of these are the objects to which one is attached; neither are wife, children, or grandchildren.
That which is truly the object of attachment is merely a heap of stinking flesh and withered bones. Because this heap exists, it gives rise to the recognition of the heap.
These deluded thoughts arise without cause, leading one to immediately form attachments.
One then claims that putrid flesh is "I," that withered bones are "I," that wife and children are "I," and that fields, houses, gold, and silk are "I. Alas! How utterly ignorant and foolish this is!
If one were a person of clear understanding who recognizes the world as having no essential reality, they would be unattached in every place. To the west lies a Buddha-land named...
Amitābha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss. Never forget this from now on; let us make a pact that it will prove essential when our very flesh and bones are scattered.
It is like a fleeting dream:
those we have as parents, wives, and children; our houses, fields, and gardens; our cattle, sheep, carriages, and horses; and even our tables, stools, and utensils.

Regarding vessels, clothing, belts, cords, and other such items—regardless of their size—whether they were inherited from one's ancestors, acquired through one's own labor, or obtained through the accumulation of efforts by one's descendants or others on one's behalf, there is nothing among them that is not one's own property.
For instance, even a window paper, though insignificant, will provoke anger if it is torn by another; and even a single needle...

Even when giving away a trifle, one still harbors a mind of stinginess. When the granaries and treasuries are full, the mind remains unsatisfied. Though gold and silks are abundant, the pursuit of them does not cease.
Every movement of the eyes and every step taken is nothing but attachment. Having stayed abroad for but a single night, one already thinks of home;
when a single servant has not yet returned, one already worries about their loss. Among all manner of affairs, there is nothing that does not hang upon the heart. One day, suddenly—
When the time limit arrives, everything must be cast away. Even this body of mine is but a discarded thing; how much more so that which lies outside the body?
Reflecting on this in silence, it is as if one were in a dream. An ancient verse says: "When impermanence arrives in a single day, one finally realizes one was but a person in a dream.
Of all things, nothing can be taken along; only karma follows one's person."
When one encounters the encumbrances of others—such as being pinched by someone or having a mouthful of spittle spat upon one's face—it is originally no great matter.
Yet, without realizing it, one gives rise to much violent anger; this inevitably leads to seeking retribution.
Furthermore, on the body, there may arise a single sore or a single carbuncle, or a rash or a patch of skin discoloration.
Although these do not inherently cause harm, the mind is nonetheless unhappy; they must reach full recovery before ceasing.
Moreover, even if bitten by a mosquito, flea, or leech, pricked by the point of a needle, or defiled by mud, filth, or dust, the mind is likewise [unhappy].
While one is joyful, when impermanence arrives and the light of the eyes closes for good, others may take this body to burn it in fire, bury it in the earth, have it bitten by dogs, or eaten by ants;
yet none can manage such a deceptive thing. How can one pointlessly suffer its entanglements?
They retreat from their faith and are unwilling to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

They regard the small for the sake of the great, and have long wandered through the cycle of birth and death within the three realms, comparing it to a prison. Thus, as long as they have not yet emerged from birth and death, they remain [in bondage].
We are prisoners within the jail of the three realms. There are three kinds of prisoners. The first kind considers themselves certain that there is no possibility of survival;

they merely seek a precarious comfort within these confines, yet as soon as the executioner arrives, they tremble in fear and meet their death. The second kind prides themselves on being the sons of those worth a thousand pieces of gold;
they do not spare their wealth as they arrange their affairs, yet their resolve is not firm, and while they are for the time being...
To steal away and enjoy the pleasures of the cauldron—if the path to rebirth is cut off and one’s way is exhausted—one must simply accept it with a willing heart.

Yet there are those of a rebellious and stubborn nature who cannot endure their bonds; they watch for a moment’s lapse in the guards’ vigilance, break free from their shackles and chains, and press forward without turning back.
Given such resolute determination, how could they ever be content to savor the remnants of life by stealing away before death, or perhaps even emerge?
[The breath] departs. How precarious are our emotions! Alas, we who dwell within the prison of the three realms may die at any year, may die at any month, may die at any day or at every moment.
The lowly die and the noble die; the old die and the young die; the wicked die and the virtuous die.
It is not according to rank, nor according to virtue, nor according to seniority. With a single breath not returning, one is immediately divided [from life].

This has been so from antiquity to the present. Yet, when a sinner enters prison, they long for release at every moment, because they know that beyond the thorny walls lies a vast world of great peace and happiness.
Likewise, sentient beings today take afflictions as their home and birth-and-death as their garden;
they do not realize that beyond this arena of the three realms, each possesses their own native land and place of bliss—the realm of the Buddhas.
Compassionately pitying this, [the Buddha] distinguished between the pure and the defiled, pointing out the path for returning to liberation.

He went back and forth through the gates of hell to prepare the way, and waited long outside the prisons to repair and refine the guest-houses. For such kindness as this, what body could possibly repay it?
Yet sentient beings, in their delusion and confusion, instead cling to these trivial matters of a mere hair’s breadth; they trade the small for the great and die without awakening. How lamentable!

When one’s body is in peril and one has but a single son, people call it a peril; yet when a son has many concubines and attendants to ensure the continuation of the lineage, why does he not consider that his own person is but one?

Is this not a peril to his very body? The world is well aware of the perils facing a son, yet it forgets the perils facing the person himself. How many levels of proficiency can be reached through the occasional essays and current-style compositions of the Seven Chapters?
Official rank; several chests of gold and silk; a house; several acres of farmland and gardens;
and several beautiful wives and concubines—all are but a single, unprincipled and trivial affair of idle gossip. Everyone is submerged by them for a lifetime.
Not a single person can escape such a trap. All their efforts have been in vain, spent in a frantic bustle;
they have already passed away. Alas, how tragic! An ancient said, "If I could turn back ten years, I might still accomplish some things.
Yet, alas, there is no principle by which the sun rises twice in this world. It is further said, "Mad schemes and far-fetched calculations all fail; there is only the frost..."
The hair at the temples comes as it was foretold. Now, if you would rest, then simply rest; if you seek the moment of realization, there will be no such moment.
These are all words of ultimate truth. Why not rouse yourself to sudden awakening and maintain single-minded right mindfulness?
Observe closely what the ancients said: "When I see another die, my heart burns like fire; it is not that I am burning for the other, but seeing this, I realize it will come to me as well.
It is also said: "The magpies peck and the crows devour until skin and flesh are gone; the wind blows and the sun scorches until the skull is dry. Look!
I previously asked those looking on to examine their own forms with care and find them startling.
Since the bodies of others are thus illusory and false, they can be seen as your own model. Your body, too, must certainly not have been cast from solid iron.
Furthermore, you have never consumed the elixir of immortality; how then could you escape impermanence? To speak of it brings fear.
Why not single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
Exert yourselves in practicing pure deeds for the sake of the world. Do not say: "I am busy now; I will wait until I have leisure," or "I am poor now;
I will wait until I am wealthy," or "I am young now; I will wait until my old age. If one's lot is fixed, one will always be busy.

It is certain that you will be impoverished; it is certain that you will meet an early death. Will you then have no opportunity for pure karma? If you suddenly perish, what can be done even if you regret it?
Therefore, while you are currently healthy and strong, strive to cultivate it now.
The Buddha said to the elder: "Human life is impermanent; it is as brief as a single breath. It is the same for the young, let alone the old.

The eyes grow dim and the ears deaf; the hair turns white and the face wrinkles; the back becomes hunched and the waist bent; the bones ache and the tendons contract; one’s gait becomes faltering and the spirit..."
Darkness and obstruction! It is like the setting sun casting its light in the west; its radiance lasts but a moment. Like withered grass welcoming autumn, it withers in an instant.
Why do you not vigorously reflect upon impermanence, exerting yourself with urgency and diligence? Why do you not contemplate the Pure Land with clarity and resolve to be reborn there?

Impermanence descends with such speed that it makes no distinction between the young and the old. While the youth remains in a state of uncertainty, for the elderly, there is certainly not much time left.
One must settle one’s worldly affairs with propriety, regardless of when the great deadline arrives.
Arriving morning and evening, one lets go of everything and proceeds; there is nothing to bind or burden one. This is the most vital point of the later years of life.
Those who cultivate the Pure Land must especially not neglect this. I have often seen people, when their breath is about to cease, still have several matters they feel unable to finish.
One must be able to maintain the intention to let go every day at the moment one goes to bed. Only then...
True. But one’s own task remains unaccomplished; it is difficult to say that one can truly let go.
When ill, one should contemplate this body: the four elements are out of harmony, the hundred bones are about to fall apart, food and drink gradually diminish, and medicine no longer has its effect.
Convenient beds and mats, groaning pillows and cushions—these are like fish swimming in a cauldron, suddenly scorched and consumed;
or like a lamp before the wind, extinguished in an instant. This body will not last long, and the path ahead is vast and obscure, its destination unknown.
Why do you not awaken with urgency, cast aside all worldly attachments, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name?
It was not during my midsummer heat that this stout and robust man suddenly met a sudden death at twilight; rather,
it was at the hour of midnight when I became aware of a stench so overpowering that one could not approach him, and we were forced to hastily prepare a coffin.
They were filled and could not wait until dawn; they were carried out for burial without any delay.
Looking at this, one who was still a robust man last evening has become nothing but a stinking corpse by morning.
A mound of grave earth. One knows not where that single consciousness-spirit has gone. A verse from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* says:
"Skin encases flesh and blood, bones wind with sinews; the deluded ordinary person recognizes this as the self. Only upon reaching death does one know it is not 'I'."
In the past, gold and jade were entrusted to others;
now, there are those who trade in them, gaining a profit of two coins for every one invested. For those traveling on the road, they reach their destination in a single day.
A journey of two days brings joy to the heart; the opposite inevitably brings sorrow. Thus, one feels anxiety or joy over the minor gains and losses of external things.
Yet, as my allotted time is finite, to let it be wasted and pass away in vain is a loss of the greatest magnitude.
Yet they do not regard this as a cause for concern. Since the conditions for the Pure Land are difficult to encounter, it is a great gain that one has fortunately come to know them;
yet they do not regard this as a cause for joy. How can their lack of reflection be so extreme!

One cannot take one's family estate or wealth with one when departing. While one’s eyes were clear and feet were strong, one engaged in worldly pursuits and calculations, guarding them with stinginess, thinking that for hundreds of thousands of millions of years one would enjoy their use.
Who would have known that all of it was merely false? Let alone anything else.
Matters of great importance are as follows: losing a single coin, breaking a chopstick, or smashing a bowl or dish;
even something as minor as a chair or table being slightly askew causes displeasure in one's heart.
Furthermore, it is like a destitute person who, when begging for a single coin or a single grain of rice, does not feel joy in his heart;

yet when the moment comes that a single breath no longer flows and both legs become rigid, even if he possesses ten thousand bolts of silk at that time, he must leave them all for others to enjoy, unable to take even a fraction with him.
What use is there in being so desperately stingy and greedy?
If you resolve to study and practice with single-minded dedication, your will must be decisive. You have spent your entire life practicing Chan;

yet, having failed to awaken through Chan, you turn now to the teachings, only to find them unclear as well. Having come to this point, your deluded thoughts remain undiminished, and you wish once more to utter a few words of Chan. Furthermore...
One must speak a few words of teaching, write a few characters, and compose a few poems. Sentiment hangs between two ends;
thoughts divide into four paths. The Patriarch said: "A hair’s breadth of attachment is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; in a mere flash, sentiment arises."
Bound for ten thousand kalpas, you nevertheless lack resolve in your will and are full of manifold thoughts. Because of these manifold thoughts, you interrupt right mindfulness.
Thus, a single thought that interrupts mindfulness is itself the karma that binds one to the three miserable realms.

Furthermore, if you guard the roots of your precepts yet your will lacks resolve—perhaps because your body and speech are, moment by moment, racing toward external pursuits—the Scripture teaches: "It would be better..."
To pour molten copper into one’s mouth is not permissible for one whose mouth has broken the precepts to receive food or drink from others;
it would be better to wrap one’s body in hot iron than for one whose body has broken the precepts to receive clothing from others.

Moreover, because the various precepts were not strictly observed, the mind of deviance moved falsely, interrupting dedicated cultivation. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself molten copper and hot iron.

This is karma. Furthermore, one fails to sever hatred and attachment; one’s resolve remains indecisive. Whenever confronted with empty fame and superficial profit, one fails to examine oneself and break through these attachments.
When fame and profit belong to oneself, greed and craving arise; when fame and profit belong to others, jealousy and hatred arise. As an ancient said:
Coveting fame is coveting profit; both lead toward the realm of hungry ghosts. Pursuing love and pursuing hatred lead equally into the fiery pit.
Yet you, because of this very love and hatred, create interruptions in your practice for the Pure Land. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of the hungry ghosts' fiery pit.
Hooked, locked, and linked like a chain, worldly affairs are manifold; the conditions of birth are ten thousandfold disturbances. Like hooks and locks, they form an unbroken chain.

The mind does not abide for even a single thought-moment, and the body never rests in any place. They enslave me in the cycle of rising and falling and obstruct my original nature, continuing from kalpa after kalpa until this very day.
It has never ceased to rest; impermanence shifts and changes, allowing nothing to remain for long. Even a lifespan of a hundred years does not exceed the snap of a finger.
Today and tomorrow cannot guarantee one's continued existence. Suddenly, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one is unaware that a moment has already given way to a different birth.
According to their karmic causes, they receive distinct forms and species—some with fur and horns, some dwelling on the earth or flying through the air.

Today, having forgotten all that they saw and understood, they are dazed and confused. Drifting through the three miserable realms and the six destinies for many kalpas, they know not where to turn; this may truly be called great suffering.

If you do not attend to this very moment before your eyes, emulating those who have attained awakening first, vigorously generating the Great Mind and establishing a resolute will to leap out from the dense forest of afflictions,
how could your practice ever become so manifest as to move the heavens and the world with its radiance, bringing grace to all beings and receiving the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas?
In such a case, you would not even wait for the exhaustion of your retribution in this Sahā world, but would immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Set aside all worldly affairs;
all things in the world are entirely like dreams, illusions, echoes, and shadows. Which single thing possesses real efficacy? Which single thing can take the place of birth and death?
Even if you were to extensively construct monasteries and greatly increase the permanent endowments, thinking that you have performed many good deeds—this, in fact, is [a delusion].

To violate the Tathāgata’s precepts and fail to realize the fundamental source of the Way, yet extensively construct monasteries and such, is to know nothing of the faults inherent in conditioned merit.
Before the heavenly realm is achieved, hell is already established; before the nature of birth and death is clarified, all such acts become the root of suffering.

When the light of the eyes falls to the ground and one undergoes retribution, only then will one realize that everything done throughout one's life was merely adding shackles to existing shackles, adding chains to existing chains.
Above, the lock is added; once the human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas. Even an iron-hearted man would shed tears upon hearing this.
Therefore, set aside all affairs and focus the mind on right mindfulness.

One day, a certain man witnessed the death of an old person and saw him before King Yama. The man reproached the king, saying, "Why did you not send word to me sooner? The king replied, "I have sent word many times.
That your eyes gradually grew dim was the first message; that your ears gradually grew deaf was the second; and that your teeth gradually fell out was the third."
Furthermore, your hundred limbs grow more decrepit day by day; you truly do not know how many such changes have occurred.

A young man also reproached the king, saying, "My eyes are clear, my ears are sharp, my teeth are strong, and my hundred limbs are robust. Why does Your Majesty not grant me your trust as well? The king said:
There are also those who believe in you, my lord; it is simply that you do not perceive them. To the east of our neighbor, there are those of forty or fifty who have died;
to the west, there are those of twenty or thirty who have died. Furthermore, there are those who die before reaching ten years of age, and even infants at the breast.
Is this not proof? A fine horse moves upon seeing the shadow of the whip; one who must wait for the needle to pierce the skin is but a hack.
"I am but a weary old horse. What lamentation can avail now?

If one practices the Way early on, one cannot serve as a high-ranking official of the first rank with two straight legs; nor can one maintain a fortune of ten thousand strings of cash with two straight legs.
When both legs are straight, filial sons and obedient grandsons cannot take their place; when both legs are straight, pampered wives and beautiful concubines cannot harbor their affections;
when both legs are straight, world-conquering schemes cannot be employed; when both legs are straight, a belly full of pearls and jewels cannot be flaunted.
With these two legs straight, one cannot eat exquisite delicacies. With these two legs straight, one cannot dwell in lofty halls or great mansions.
With these two legs straight, one cannot wear silks and brocades filling the chests. With these two legs straight, one cannot carry precious playthings filling the baskets.
With these two legs straight, one cannot enjoy exquisite dances and pure songs. With these two legs straight, one cannot roam by green waters and blue mountains.
With these two legs straight, one cannot avoid creating the karmic offenses of the lower realms. With these two legs straight, one cannot resolve the enmity of those one has provoked.
With both feet set straight, one cannot avoid the attendants of Yama; with both feet set straight, one cannot deflect them with clever words or flowery speech;
with both feet set straight, one cannot employ the levers of human sentiment; with both feet set straight, one cannot rely on the power of relatives.
With legs straight as a blade, one cannot escape the Hell of Flaming Wheels; with legs straight as a horse’s belly, one cannot hide from the womb of a donkey.

Straight! Straight! Straight! It does not wait for a season nor for a day; the hour of noon does not guarantee the hour of the fifth watch, and midday does not guarantee the hour of the seventh watch.
Even if your achievements rival those of the Duke of Ji, even if your heroism rivals that of Xiang Yu—no matter who you may be.
May your wealth surpass that of Shi Chong; may your literary talent surpass that of Li Bai; may you possess the myriad tongues of Su Qin;
may you employ the sixfold stratagems of Chen Ping; may you possess the skill of Li Lou and Gongshu Ban; may you master the arts of Guan Lu and Zhang Junping.
Let your royal power reach the heavens; let your consorts’ beauty topple the state. Yet in the throat there is but three inches of breath, while the shoulders labor in vain with a thousand efforts.
Yesterday you strode the streets displaying your radiant countenance; tonight you lie within the coffin as a withered bone.
Upon the Northern Mang Hills, how many tombs rise and fall—owls hoot through the night and green maples weep. Through a thousand years, empires rise and fall.
A hive for bees and ants; a den of foxes where a hundred years of rise and fall unfold. Casting aside wholesome thoughts without reflection, one loses this human body, difficult to find again.
Though wealth and honor are surely the result of past lives, even when enjoying them, one must guard against the exhaustion of one’s allotted lifespan.
Holding the hundred-and-eighth mani jewel in the hand, remember the single phrase of Amitābha in the heart. If not delivered in this life, when will you be delivered? Practice!
Life passes quickly and impermanence presses hard; children and grandchildren are all but karmic creditors. Wealth and fame are all honey upon the edge of a blade;
killing living beings is devouring the flesh of one’s own kin. Sexual lust and depravity are drinking molten copper. When climbing into bed, one must take leave of one’s shoes and socks;
whether one will return tomorrow is uncertain. With a single cry of departure, one can only follow along. To pray to deities or worship the Buddha is but a hair’s breadth [of help].
It is of no avail. Even one's closest kin—father and son, or husband and wife—may be reborn in altered forms, returning so changed that one recognizes them not.

When the boat reaches Qutang Gorge, it is too late to patch its leaks; many precious days and years have been squandered. The principles of saṃsāra are clear in every detail; the workings of cause and effect never fail.
To be deluded through many lifetimes and yet claim the present life alone is one’s own—how many such fools there are who all cry out in grievance! Call upon [the Buddha] repeatedly!
Though I earnestly exhorted him, he would not turn his mind back; it seems he must simply wait until his two feet become straight.

By nature, Buddhas and sentient beings are interconnected; they share the same source of awakening. Although delusion and enlightenment differ, their underlying principle is eternally equal. Therefore, all Buddhas are...
The Buddhas are within the minds of sentient beings; sentient beings are the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas.
Speaking from this perspective, the essential spirit of the Buddhas and the minds of sentient beings is never not in mutual resonance.

Yet, while the Buddhas at no time do not desire to deliver sentient beings, sentient beings, moment after moment, remain deluded and turn their backs upon them. As a sutra says: "One person focuses entirely on remembering; the other person focuses entirely on forgetting."

If you meet her, it is as if you had not met; if you see her, it is as if you had not seen. If you, my son, remember your mother as she remembers you, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall never be separated or far apart.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.

He is not far from the Buddha. It is precisely because of the equality of this single principle and the mutual connection of our innate nature that he is able to spontaneously uproot suffering and bestow happiness.
How much more so for Amitāyus Buddha, who, while practicing the causal path, made forty-eight vows, vowing to attain Sukhāvatī and gather in sentient beings.
One need only have deep faith and mindfulness, repeatedly making the vow to be born in the Western Land. As...
A magnet and a needle spontaneously attract one another; yet while a magnet can attract iron, it cannot attract copper.
This is analogous to how a Buddha can deliver those with whom he has a karmic connection, but cannot deliver sentient beings who lack such a connection.

It is easier to be moved by Amitābha than by other Buddhas—is this not because the vows of the living being and the Buddha are interrelated? Therefore, those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land must have faith.
The three—practice, vows, and aspiration—are indispensable; none may be lacking.

To understand birth and death through the ten kinds of faith and desire, one should cultivate pure karma by giving rise to these ten kinds of faith, keeping them in mind at all times without forgetfulness, and resolving to be born [in the Pure Land].
In the Pure Land, one attains non-retrogression. First, one believes that all teachings spoken by the Buddha are the sincere words of his golden mouth;
they are true and not false. Second, one believes that ordinary beings remain in delusion; their consciousness does not perish, and they circulate through the six realms of existence without ceasing.

Third, one believes that practicing in this land, as long as the fruits of the Path have not been attained, one cannot escape saṃsāra. Fourth, one believes that as long as one has not emerged from saṃsāra, even if born in the heavens, one remains there.
1. One cannot avoid falling [into lower realms]. 2. Those sentient beings who believe in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) shall never again fall back once they are born there.
3. Those sentient beings who believe and make a vow to be born in the Pure Land will certainly attain rebirth there. 4.

Those sentient beings who believe that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas. 5. Those sentient beings who believe that Amitābha Buddha employs his supernormal powers for those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).

Radiant Light. To embrace and not abandon those who practice the ninefold mindfulness of the Buddha: the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall at all times protect and mind them with their spiritual powers.
Once the tenth faith has arisen, one will reach the Pure Land, where one’s lifespan is immeasurable, and in a single lifetime, one shall attain unsurpassed bodhi.
If one cannot have deep faith in these ten points and gives rise to doubt and confusion, then even though one practices mindfulness...
If one does not attain rebirth in the Pure Land, then even though one is a Buddha, one will not go there.

For those who practice the Pure Land path on Mount Sumeru, it is absolutely necessary to confront birth and death; it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then leaving it at that. One must truly do so.
Reflect upon the swiftness of impermanence; time does not wait for anyone. You must take this as a single, unified task before you can succeed.

If you advance half-heartedly and retreat half-heartedly, if you are neither fully believing nor fully doubting, what possible benefit will this bring? How can you escape the cycle of saṃsāra? It is like a load of one hundred and twenty catties:
when the time comes, you must be able to carry it yourself; only then will the matter be resolved. It will certainly not do otherwise.
It does not lie in eloquent speech or clever discourse to widely transform sentient beings; it certainly does not lie in the transmission of doctrines or the fabrication of artificial performances.
It certainly does not lie in the grand establishment of ritual sites or the lighting of many incense sticks and candles.
If you can truly believe this, then from this very day forward, arouse great courage and great diligence. Do not concern yourself with whether you understand or not; see your own nature.
Do not seek to perceive the nature; simply uphold a single phrase of the Buddha. Be like one leaning against Mount Sumeru, unshakable and immovable.
With single-minded focus and intense vigor, vow to spend this entire life together ascending to the Pure Land.
Regarding the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): with the power of knowing others' minds, the Buddha knows their thoughts; with the power of the divine ear, the Buddha hears their words;
and with the power of the divine eye, the Buddha sees their physical prostrations. Thus, those who possess faith...
It is like a fruit tree planted deeply; because its roots are firm, it is unmoved by the wind, and later, bearing fruit, it relieves the hunger and thirst of people.
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are likewise thus.

Regarding the practice of dedicating merit toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it is simply a matter of valuing true faith. First, one must believe that I am a Buddha-to-be, while Amitābha is a Buddha who has already attained completion;
their essence is non-dual. Next, one must believe that this Sahā world is indeed suffering, and that the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is...
One can thus return home. With fervent joy and aversion, one next believes that every single movement of the present moment can be dedicated toward the Western Land.
If one does not dedicate [merit], even superior-grade goodness will not lead to rebirth there.

If one knows how to dedicate, even if one has mistakenly committed evil deeds, by swiftly severing the continuity of such thoughts and giving rise to earnest and profound repentance, the power of that repentance can also enable one to attain rebirth.
How much more so for those who maintain the precepts, cultivate merit, and perform various superior deeds—how could these not suffice to adorn the Pure Land?

It is simply because the power of one's faith is not deep that these superior deeds sink into the realm of outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, to wish to abandon this and seek another path is a profound error.
One need only increase one’s true faith; as for all other practices and conduct, there is no need to change them at all.

If one wishes to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, one must first give rise to faith. Without faith, one will achieve nothing at all. One should have the conviction that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly lead to birth in the Pure Land;

the conviction that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly extinguish all transgressions; the conviction that mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly secure the protection of the Buddhas; [and the conviction that] mindfulness of the Buddha...
One will certainly attain the realization of Buddhahood. One must believe that at the time of death, the Buddha will surely come to welcome one.

One must believe that those who share this faith in the Buddha will all attain rebirth in the Pure Land. One must believe that those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression.

One must believe that through the recitation of the Buddha's name, one will be born in the Pure Land and will certainly not fall into the three evil realms. By upholding this Dharma, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.
Nowadays, although people may give rise to the aspiration for the Way, they are burdened by three things— the body, speech, and the concerns of family and livelihood—
and thus spend their entire lives in busyness, turmoil, suffering, and futility, passing them all in vain.

Throughout one's life, one cannot practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, because of these burdens, one gives rise to immeasurable greed, anger, and delusion, thereby committing immeasurable great and small evil karmas.

A person of resolve should, from this very day and this very moment, realize that this body is false and that these relatives and household affairs are all illusory. Regarding these three kinds of burdens, do not identify with them; do not...

Do not be attached; do not crave attachment. You must give rise from within your own breast a single heart of faith that does not change even if the mountains crumble, nor shift even if the oceans dry up.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, simply maintain single-minded right mindfulness at all times.
You must be courageous and no longer procrastinate; you must be diligent and never indolent; you must be steadfast and never again...
Do not neglect this; simply let the light of reflection shine back upon it to pierce through [delusion]. Reflect with deep self-examination. Think of it today, think of it tomorrow.
When the time arrives, you will surely see the Buddha; you will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Reflect deeply and believe with certainty;

this is the essential gateway for entering the Path. Faith is the foremost. For example, when a thief in the world is eventually exposed by the authorities, they do not fail to subject him to the ultimate punishment.
Yet, once he has been released, he continues as before without remorse. Why is this so? It is because of others.
This teaching is a path that, if one truly believes it, requires no written texts and not even a single coin of capital, yet yields immeasurable profit.

For this reason, though we have endured all manner of suffering and pain, we must resolutely never retreat or regret. Those who recite the Buddha's name today are unwilling to apply themselves with earnest diligence;

this is simply because they have never deeply contemplated or sincerely believed in this Dharma-gate. Without expending much effort, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain, and the vision of the Buddha is assured.
The Buddha Amitābha currently resides in the Western Quarter, teaching and transforming countless devas, humans, and sentient beings, down to the most minute crawling and flying insects;
there are none who do not attain transcendence and liberation. "Crawling and flying" refers to tiny flying insects.
Even wriggling insects—referring here to minute maggots—are still transformed and delivered by the Buddha; how much more so for human beings!
This is why he extensively delivers sentient beings without end or limit. If a person takes refuge even for a single thought-moment, they will consequently be born in that land;
there is no need for doubt.

To seek amnesty and return to the status of a commoner is like iron or stone: though heavy, it relies upon a boat; by the power of the vessel, one can cross the river. A single needle, though light, cannot cross the river without relying on a boat or ship.
Thus, when a person has grave offenses, if they rely upon the power of the Buddha, they may be reborn in the Pure Land. As for their sins...
Although an evil deed may be slight, it cannot lead to rebirth there without relying on the power of the Buddha.

It is like a thief who, having lived his life as such, is granted amnesty one day and subsequently becomes a virtuous citizen; those who rely on the power of the Buddha to extinguish their sins and evils are just like this.

Furthermore, it is like lice and fleas that die and are reborn ten thousand times yet cannot travel even a single *li*; if they attach themselves to a human body, they can reach a distance of a thousand *li*. Relying on the power of the Buddha is likewise so.
It is exactly the same for those who are born in the Pure Land; what further cause for doubt could there be?

It is not surprising that those bound by their own perceptions often fail to believe when they suddenly hear descriptions of the Pure Land’s scenery. This is because they are constrained by what their eyes have seen.
It is merely what has been seen previously. For instance, how can those who dwell in humble alleys and dwellings of filth know of the purity of grand palatial halls?
How can those who eat from small vessels and subsist on coarse herbs know of the ten-foot-square dining hall before a meal?

How can those who store but a few grains in tattered baskets know of the overflowing abundance of the imperial treasury? Therefore, dwelling in this turbid world, one does not believe that [such things exist].
The pure Buddha-fields. [Beings here] are born from a womb, unaware that there exists birth by transformation from lotuses;
their lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, unaware that there exist lifespans as vast as the sands of the Ganges;

clothing and food must depend on labor, unaware that there exists natural clothing and food; and their happiness is constantly intermingled with sorrow and affliction, unaware that [there exists] that [purity].
There is a singular, absolute happiness. Thus, that which the Buddha has spoken cannot be disbelieved simply because it is not visible before one's eyes;
there is no proof [to the contrary].
Among the people of this world, there are some who practice yet find no efficacy. This is because their faculty of faith is shallow and thin;

their ground is not true, and they have never established their practice. First desiring to be known by others, they are inwardly self-conceited and outwardly seek to appear brilliant, hoping that others will show them respect and provide offerings so that they may gain something.
They even go so far as to speak falsely, claiming to have seen pure realms or to have perceived some slight anomaly.

Regarding these [inauspicious signs], as well as auspicious signs in dreams, if one does not yet discern whether they are favorable or unfavorable, and first wishes to explain such inferior occurrences, one will certainly be deluded by Māra.
One’s vows and practices will then decline and be lost, leading one back to follow the miserable realms of birth and death. Is it not necessary to be cautious?

Deceiving oneself through arrogance and abandoning the world, there are those who give rise to three kinds of faithless thoughts and fail to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land], which is truly lamentable. The first is:
"I shall transcend the Buddhas and the Patriarchs; the Pure Land is not a place where I ought to be born. The second is: "Everywhere is a pure land; the Western [Pure Land] is not necessary."
Third, it is said: "The holy realm of Ultimate Bliss—beings such as ourselves, ordinary worldlings, cannot be born there.
Now, the ocean of practice is inexhaustible, as seen in the vows of Samantabhadra; though the land of Amitābha Buddha may seem empty, Vimalakīrti constantly cultivated the Pure Land.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions offer praise with their broad tongues, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the aspiration to go there together. Try to reflect for yourself: who among us can compare with these?
"Sages! To say that rebirth is not possible is what kind of self-deception it is! Take for instance the patriarch Nāgārjuna: the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic record of him.
As for Vasubandhu, the founder of the doctrinal school, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* contains verses on seeking rebirth.

Master Ci'en, in his *General Praise*, first mentions the 'Ten Superiorities'; Master Zhiyi, in analyzing the principles, clearly resolves the 'Ten Doubts. All of them were supreme sages of refined wisdom."
To advance toward rebirth in the Pure Land while claiming it is not necessary—how self-deprecating that is! One can extinguish the fire-chariots [of hell], and a boat with stones will not sink.
As for those who manifest immediate karmic rewards, none surpass Zhang Kui’s ten recitations; yet he transcended to a supreme place, while others entered hell.
Nothing is swifter than the heroic and sagacious who, having revived once more, realize the wondrous cause. The transgressions of worldly people may not necessarily be like this;

yet to say that one cannot be reborn—how self-abandoning is that! To deceive oneself, to be arrogant toward oneself, and to abandon one's own spiritual nature, thereby flowing into the cycle of saṃsāra—whose fault is this?

According to the Original Vow of the Meritorious Amitābha: "If sentient beings of the ten directions desire to be born in my land and, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, recite my name even ten times, yet fail to achieve this, I vow not to attain Buddhahood.
If those who have faith and joy through even ten recitations can still attain rebirth, how much more so for those who practice for a single day?"
If this is so for those who have faith and joy, how much more so for those who have faith and joy for one month, one year, or even for a single lifetime?

A single thought-moment extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; how much more so ten such thoughts? How much more so the sins extinguished by recollecting the Buddha for one day, one month, one year, or a single lifetime?
If even grave sins are extinguished, how much more so minor sins? Furthermore, let us calculate and compare the merit of recollection.
Regarding the comparison between the Buddha’s merits and other roots of goodness in terms of their relative superiority or inferiority, a sutra states:

"If a person were to provide the four types of most excellent offerings to fill the great trichiliocosm with Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, the merit thereby obtained would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the merit gained by another person who joins their palms and recites the name of the Buddha once; it cannot be measured by calculation or analogy."

It cannot be matched. If the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name even once is already such, how much more so the merit of ten recitations, or of reciting the Buddha’s name for a day, a month, a year, or an entire lifetime!
In this present life, one will be at peace and secure; the various sages will protect one, and one will be free from all calamities and misfortunes.
His merit is immeasurable.

The Buddha, King of Dharma, fills the worlds of the ten directions with Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vibuddha*). Yet, due to my inverted perceptions, I have drifted in and out of birth and death.
How is it that through a single thought-moment one attains rebirth in the Pure Land? The karma I have created since beginningless time originally arises from a single thought-moment;
since it arises from a single thought-moment, it likewise ceases through a single thought-moment. At the point where arising and ceasing are utterly extinguished, I and the Buddha are identical.

The focus of a person's thoughts is most critical; it is like water rushing toward the sea, fire flaring upward, a sharp blade inevitably wounding, or a poisonous drug inevitably taking effect—none of these fail to reach their destination. The mindfulness of the Buddha is just the same.
One should know that the power of mindfulness is the king among all dharmas.
With this single thought, focusing the mind on a single thought, one holds to a single phrase of the Buddha's name. This very single thought is my original teacher; it is the manifested Buddha.
It is the valiant general who shatters hell; it is the precious sword that slays all evils; it is the light that opens up the darkness.
The lamp is the great vessel for crossing the sea of suffering; it is the excellent remedy for liberation from birth and death;
it is the path for exiting the three realms; it is the Amitābha of one’s own nature; and it is the attainment of the Pure Land of Mind-Only. One must simply remember this:
keep the single phrase of the Buddha’s name in mind and do not let it be lost. Let it be ever-present in every thought-moment, never departing from the mind. Thus it is.
Be mindful; it is clear and not obscure. Why, then, must you ask others for the way home?

To be the master of one's own mind, yet to harbor afflictions in every thought, is the very root of the suffering of birth and death. Now, by means of a single recitation of the Buddha’s name, one can extinguish these afflictions. Thus...

This Buddha is the one who delivers beings from the suffering of birth and death. If you can eliminate afflictions by recollecting the Buddha, you will then be able to bring an end to birth and death;

there is no other method. If you recollect the Buddha until you attain mastery over your afflictions, you will attain mastery even within dreams, and you will attain mastery amidst the suffering of illness, until at the moment of death you know where you shall go.
This matter is not difficult to practice; it simply requires that one’s resolve regarding birth and death be urgent.

Relying single-mindedly on the recitation of the Buddha's name alone, without seeking or reflecting upon anything else, after a long time of pure cultivation, one will naturally attain great peace and joy, and achieve great benefit.
Take this single phrase of the Buddha as your very life-force and hold it across your chest. Make it your life-force; clench your teeth with determination and never let go.
Even while eating, drinking, rising, resting, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this one sound of "Buddha" shall be ever-present before you at all times.

If you encounter circumstances that are adverse or favorable, or experiences of joy or anger, and your mind becomes unsettled, simply take up the single phrase "Buddha" and apply it with forceful pressure.
Immediately, the present circumstances will be seen for what they are and will vanish on the spot.
To practice the true object with true mindfulness of the Buddha, one must possess six kinds of mindfulness. First is courageous mindfulness. If you are too weak-willed, it will not do;

you must be like a filial son seeking to avenge a deep grievance against his parents. Even if it requires traversing high cliffs, deep ravines, ghostly paths, or tiger dens, you must go forth without fear.

Therefore, there is first the thought of sorrowful grief: it comes with such overwhelming intensity that whenever one thinks of the Buddha, the hair on one's body stands on end and the five internal organs feel as if they would tear apart, like remembering a compassionate mother from whom one was separated for a short time, or a wise son who has passed away. There is secondly the thought of poignant indignation:

it comes with such profound tranquility that it cannot be compared to the desolation of a failed candidate, solitary and destitute, whose talent remains unappreciated; yet whenever one brings this to mind, [the emotion wells up].

First, the thought of longing and attachment, because one fears not wishing to live; due to excessive detachment, one cannot obtain objects as deeply loved as oneself, so that in both soul and dream one remains entangled, fearing only the possibility of losing them. Second, the thought of exultant joy when pleasant things appear before one.

It is like a cold person obtaining clothing or a hungry person obtaining food; it is like one whose face is struck by an evil omen and who feels such intense regret that they feel as though they have escaped from the jaws of death.
In short, when mind and mouth are one, and every word flows forth from the very marrow of one's bones, only then is this the true realm of *nianfo*.
The present mind that is capable of recitation—Zhang San and Li Si—is fundamentally free from fault and beyond all conceptualization; there is no need to deliberately strive for such freedom.

The Buddha who is presently being recited is fundamentally transcendent of emotion and beyond all calculation; why labor to speak of the subtle or discuss the profound? It is simply a matter of being able to believe.

Once you have attained stability in your practice, proceed directly with recitation—whether ten thousand times a day and night, or five thousand, or three thousand—taking it as your standard that this be done with absolute consistency and without fail until the end of this life, vowing never to change your resolve.

If today you are "Zhang San" and tomorrow you are "Li Si," if you encounter those of the Scriptural Teachings (Jiaoxia) you again think of searching for chapters and picking out phrases; if you encounter those of the Zen School (Zongmen) you again think of investigating and scrutinizing. [This must not happen.]

Question and answer: Upon meeting a person who upholds the Vinaya, one further reflects on donning the robes and using the alms bowl; thus, everything becomes unresolved and every account remains unclear.
Let it all go.
First, completely set aside and let go of all the chaotic thoughts within your chest until there is nowhere left to let them go.
Solely lift up one phrase of the Buddha’s name, making it vivid and distinct, uninterrupted in the mind.

It should be like a string threading through beads, or like the nock of an arrow meeting the tip of the shaft, with not even a hair’s breadth of space between them. Exert yourself in this manner and remain steadfastly fixed upon it. At that moment—
In all circumstances, one is not led astray or distracted by external conditions. Whether in daily activities or stillness, there is neither confusion nor disorder;
even in dreams it remains as it is, naturally becoming a single, seamless whole.

If you are truly earnest about birth and death, and if every thought-moment is as urgent as if your head were on fire, you must fear that once this human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it even in a hundred million kalpas.
Bite down firmly upon this single sound of "Buddha" and resolve to overcome it; let it manifest in every place and at every thought-moment so that you are not obstructed by delusive thoughts.
By applying such bitter and earnest effort for a long time, you will eventually reach a state of pure mastery.
Spontaneous resonance occurs; without seeking to form a continuous state, it naturally becomes one. To pursue deluded thoughts is the disease;
reciting the Buddha’s name is the medicine. A chronic illness cannot be cured by a single dose, nor can accumulated delusions be eliminated in an instant.
The principle is one: mindfulness alone can eliminate them. Do not concern yourself with the proliferation of deluded thoughts;

it is simply vital that your recitation of the Buddha’s name be earnest and precise, with every syllable distinct and every phrase continuous. Only by maintaining this with all your might will you have a portion of progress toward the goal.
Maintain constant mindfulness with close and continuous attention. Let not the mind’s recollection pass in vain. Day after day, moment after moment, do not let it slip away.

Be persistent and uninterrupted, like a hen brooding over her eggs, always ensuring that the warmth continues without ceasing; this is precisely what is meant by the succession of pure mindfulness. Furthermore, augment this with wisdom.
Upon illumination, one realizes that the Pure Land is none other than one's own mind. This is the practice for those of superior intelligence.

When awakening through loud chanting, it requires great effort; when reciting silently, one easily falls into dullness. It is simply a matter of maintaining a continuous and dense flow, with the sound present.
The space between the lips and teeth is indeed where the Vajradhara resides; yet, one must not grasp at this as being fixed.

If one beats fish eggs with the hand while shouting along with the mouth, no benefit will be gained. It is essential that every phrase leave the mouth and enter the ear, and every sound awaken the mind of self.
For example, if one person is in deep sleep and another calls out, "O [Name]," the sleeper will immediately wake up.
Thus, among all practices, the recitation of the Buddha's name is most capable of gathering the mind.

One may practice true recitation, loud recitation, low-voiced recitation, the six-character recitation, the four-character recitation, rapid recitation, slow recitation, clear recitation, or silent recitation.
Recite with palms joined; recite while kneeling; recite facing the Buddha; recite facing west; recite while striking the wooden board; recite while striking the fish-shaped gong;
recite while counting beads on a rosary; recite while walking the meditation path; recite while prostrating; recite alone; recite together with the assembly; recite at home; recite abroad;
recite in leisure; recite in busyness; recite while walking; recite while standing; recite while sitting; recite while lying down—even within dreams.
One should also contemplate thus: contemplate until one’s heart is pierced with sorrow and tears flow; contemplate until the fire is extinguished and the ashes grow cold;

contemplate until gods wail and ghosts weep; contemplate until the heavens rejoice and the deities are delighted. With a single utterance of "Buddha," the palaces of the Māra kings are shaken to their foundations.

One utterance of "Buddha" shatters the Forest of Swords and Mountains of Blades. One utterance of "Buddha" eliminates karmic obstructions accumulated over hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
One utterance of "Buddha" opens the causes and conditions for the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence.
For a beginner at the very start, one must use a prayer bead rosary to keep things clearly in mind and establish a fixed schedule that is never missed.

After practicing for a long time until it becomes natural and effortless, one will recite spontaneously even without thinking of it; at that point, it is acceptable whether one keeps count or not. If...
From the very beginning, people insist on speaking only pleasant words; they seek to avoid attachment to forms and desire to study the perfect, harmonious, and autonomous state.

This is entirely because their faith is not deep and their practice is not vigorous. Even if you can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures and deliver the seventeen hundred turning phrases, these are all matters pertaining to the shore of birth and death. At the moment of death, none of them will be of any use.
Like surging waves and billowing tides,
young practitioners of the new learning, as soon as they take up a single phrase of the Buddha and fix it upon their minds, find their idle thoughts and delusions boiling over even more intensely.
They then claim that the practice of *nienfo* cannot still the mind, failing to realize that this has been the nature of your birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas.
As for the root cause, how can it be severed immediately? Furthermore, at the moment when myriad thoughts fly about in confusion, this is precisely the time to apply the practice.
As they scatter, they are gathered back; as they scatter, they are gathered back. After a long period of such cultivation, one becomes proficient, and delusive thoughts will naturally cease to arise.
Moreover, that which enables you to perceive these delusive thoughts is this very Buddha. If you do not recite the Buddha’s name, [the mind] will surge like a surging tide. At that moment—
How could one who is not still ever attain awakening?

The Tathāgata’s ceaseless teaching for people to practice Buddha-recollection is precisely to gather hundreds of thousands of myriad distracted thoughts into a single thought. Within that single thought, one must be fiercely diligent.

They naturally realized Buddhahood. Yet when we consider people today who practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name), amidst their single string of plain prayer beads, thoughts arise and cease in countless shifts;
thus, their nianfo is merely a murmuring of the lips, while in their hearts they are entirely unaware of the Buddha.
Since their hands do not accord with their mouths, and their mouths do not accord with their hearts, how can one expect such ordinary people to achieve anything?
Can one merge with the Buddha to become one?
A verse from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a person vows to attain Buddhahood and calls upon Amitābha, he will immediately appear before them."
Because of his body, I take refuge and pay homage. If there are those who wish to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, they should, with a heart of reverence, uphold and recite his name.
If one plants roots of goodness but harbors doubt, the flower will not bloom; for those whose faith is pure, the flower blooms and they immediately behold the Buddha.

There are five ways to practice the dharma with reverent respect. First, one should revere the Buddha, who is the honored one with whom one has a karmic connection; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or attending to the necessities of nature, one should always protect the direction of the west.
Second, one should revere the image and teaching with which one has a karmic connection; this includes setting up an image of Amitābha and upholding his teachings. Third, one should revere...

One should respectfully approach and draw near to one's teachers and spiritual friends, as they serve as conditions for progress. Fourth, one should respect fellow students—that is, those who practice the same pure deeds—so that they may mutually encourage and benefit one another.
Fifth, one should always revere the Triple Gem, as it serves as the supreme condition for one’s birth [in favorable states]. One should cultivate such reverence in this manner.
One will certainly attain rebirth there.

By gathering the six sense faculties with single-minded right mindfulness, all six faculties are gathered; thus, all six bases are mindful. For example, when the eye does not grasp at forms, this is the eye [in its true state].
Recite the Buddha’s name. When the ears hear no sounds, this is the ears reciting the Buddha’s name. When the nose smells no odors, this is the nose reciting the Buddha’s name.
When the mind thinks of no dharmas, this is the mind reciting the Buddha’s name. Because all six sense faculties are thus fully gathered, pure mindfulness can proceed in succession.
Without needing further expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind and manifests the vision of the Buddha before oneself.

To achieve accomplishment within a fixed period, the practitioner who wishes to attain realization by a specific deadline must immediately set aside all mundane affairs and miscellaneous duties. One should simply maintain the thought that before long, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land;
one should revile and abandon craving and desire, diligently still anger and delusion, and swiftly seek to cast off beginningless evil habits.
Do not let this become an obstacle; you should observe for yourself which practice is predominant, then censure and abandon it to bring them into balance.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* clarifies a period of seven weeks, the *Dundubhisvara-rāja Sūtra* clarifies ten days and ten nights, and the *Amitābha Sūtra* clarifies seven days.

Taking these three standards as the limit, perform prostrations and repentance before the Buddha during the six periods of day and night, without letting even a single snap of the fingers pass in vain.
Recently, when reflecting on the five worldly desires or engaging with outsiders in speech, laughter, and frivolous discourse, I must not use such matters as pretexts for delay.
I shall abandon negligence and sleep; with single-minded devotion and without sparing even my own body or life, I shall resolutely undertake pure karma so that it may be accomplished immediately.
Whether in stillness or movement, during the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—one may apply the mind at all times; yet, sitting is the most excellent.

However, for a beginner, one must first practice walking meditation more than sitting. If one is overly attached to sitting, the mind will become dull and unable to progress. This applies whether there is business to attend to or not.
One may apply the mind, yet it is best to remain free from affairs. First practice in a quiet place; later, refine yourself amidst movement.

To cultivate the body with single-mindedness, you must exclusively pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and not intermingle this with other forms of worship. Your speech must likewise exclusively recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Do not invoke other names; the intention must be to focus one's thoughts exclusively on Amitābha Buddha and do not practice other meditations.

If one practices with single-minded devotion, ten will be reborn for every ten who practice, and a hundred for every hundred. However, among those who practice various miscellaneous virtues and merely dedicate them toward rebirth in the Pure Land, not even one or two out of a thousand or ten thousand will succeed.
Now, there are people who offer three thousand prostrations to Amitābha daily and recite the name of Amitābha every day.

There have been spiritual verifications for those who recite one hundred thousand times day and night while practicing seated meditation and single-mindedly contemplating Amitābha. However, for lay bodhisattvas who perform their daily recitations morning and evening, who revere the Buddha and uphold the precepts, yet must attend to household affairs every day and are unable to practice with single-minded devotion— [The following text continues: ...the merit is not as great.
