One must rise early to burn incense, pay homage to the Triple Gem, and recite the Buddha’s name as one pleases.

Every evening, one should likewise perform prostrations and recitation as a regular daily practice. Should one ever have business that causes a lapse in this schedule, one must personally repent before the Buddha on the following day.
This dharma gate is essential and shall not interfere with one's primary vocation; beyond these morning and evening devotions, one may further engage in two...
During the six periods of the day, steal even a moment of time to recite [the name] a hundred thousand times, taking sincere devotion as your practice and aspiring to be born in the Pure Land.
For laypeople with ten recitations, who are busy and distracted by worldly affairs, every morning after dressing, face west with palms joined and recite:
A Buddha [is invoked] with one full breath as a single recitation. Ten such recitations are performed according to the length of the breath;
the breath serves as the measure of completion. The sound of the recitation is neither too high nor too low, but adjusted to be moderate.

These ten recitations are continuous and uninterrupted, the intention being to prevent the mind from scattering and to take focused diligence as the practice. This clearly demonstrates that the mind is bound by means of the breath.

With the mind and breath mutually dependent, gather the mind to recite the Buddha’s name. To achieve samādhi, counting the breath is most essential. Whenever sitting, first visualize your own body within a circle of light;
silently observe the tip of the nose and contemplate the inhalation and exhalation. For every breath, silently recite the Buddha’s name once. Only then—
Then, regulate the breath, neither too lax nor too forceful. Let the mind and the breath rely upon one another, following its inhalation and exhalation.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, practice this at all times; do not allow it to be interrupted. Constantly maintain it in secret until you enter deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

When both breath and thought are forgotten, this very body and mind become equal to empty space. After a long time of such pure mastery, the eye of the mind opens and the *samādhi* suddenly manifests.
That which manifests before you is precisely the Pure Land of Mind-Only.

You should keep in mind that for those who aspire to be reborn there, provided they can maintain single-mindedness without distraction and uphold the Name, they will not fail to reach their goal and shall likewise attain birth in that land. Why?
Only after the retribution of the physical body has been fulfilled will one be able to be born there.

You should know that Amitābha Buddha’s guidance of sentient beings to enable them to leave the ocean of suffering exceeds even that of a compassionate parent. In previous kalpas, he already established great vows:

there was no suffering he would not endure, no practice he would not perfect, no aspiration he would not establish, and no Dharma he would not teach. For the sake of delivering me, he employed hundreds of thousands of skillful means; now...

"It is indeed the right time. With unblinking eyes, he has lowered his arms and waited for me for ten kalpas. Moment by moment, he has never abandoned me, feeling a pain more acute than having his heart torn out.
His resolve has become so fervent that he enters the cycle of birth and death, traversing all three miserable realms. He does not shrink from the exhaustion of the fierce fires of hell.
If I were to turn my mind toward the Buddha, like a child longing for its mother, it would truly comfort what he holds in his heart. Thus [he spoke].
Without exceeding a single thought-moment, one shall immediately attain rebirth. Why must one necessarily pass through the interval of ten recitations before attaining rebirth?

Sit upright in a quiet room for contemplation; sweep away all external conditions and burdens, sever the dust of worldly attachments, and stare wide-eyed so that the mind does not cling to external objects.
Without dwelling in internal concentration, turn the light back for a single glance; both within and without are simultaneously stilled. Then, silently and continuously raise the thought:
"Namo Amitābha Buddha" three or five times. Turn the light back and look at yourself, saying: "To see one's nature is to become a Buddha.
Ultimately, which of these is my own original-nature Amitābha? Again, examine and observe: this very thought that is being raised right now.
From where does it arise? Penetrate this single thought; penetrate it again. Who is it that performs this penetration?
After a long while, again bring up the recitation of the Buddha's name. Again, look thus; investigate thus. Diligently apply the practice without allowing for interruption.
Remain alert and unclouded, like a hen brooding over her eggs. Whether engaged in the four modes of deportment, continue to bring it up in this way and investigate in this way.
"Enter. Suddenly, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or when hearing sounds and seeing forms, there is a sudden, clear awakening. One personally beholds the Original Nature Amitābha;
body and mind, internal and external, are simultaneously liberated. The entire earth is this Western Land; the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are none other than oneself.
In stillness, there is no lack of illumination; in movement, one does not depart from quiescence."
It is studied that saṃsāra has craving as its root. Yet, though this craving is restrained by a hundred means, it cannot be extinguished.
Although the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is its direct antidote, ordinary worldlings at the stage of the "vast ground" have heavy obstructions and deep defilements; they see only—
When pure, one does not perceive impurity. One contemplates the subtle and refined nature of dharmas, yet few are able to achieve success.
If this is so, what should be done? The Sūtra says: "Desire arises from your mind; the mind arises from thought. Now, observe this thought: from where does it arise again?
Examine it, investigate it, and investigate it without ceasing. It is like a rat entering a cow’s horn; there must inevitably be a point of reversal and resolution.

Directly and simply, throughout the twelve periods of the day, hold to one phrase of the Buddha’s name; let your thoughts be focused and your contemplation serene. Furthermore, turn the light back upon yourself to examine:
"What is my original nature? When the four elements separate, where will I go? Constantly maintain this doubt until, suddenly, you recognize it.
One then knows the place where one may settle the body and establish one's life; this is precisely the direct path of cultivation.

With a single-minded heart, take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May his pure light illumine me; may his compassionate vow [protect me].
Gather me in. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata for the sake of the path to Bodhi, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

According to the Buddha’s original vow: "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land and, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, invoke my name even ten times, yet are not born there, may I not attain perfect awakening.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, may I enter the presence of the Tathāgata.
Within the ocean of great vows, by relying on the compassionate power of the Buddha, all transgressions are extinguished and the pure causes increase.

When approaching the end of life, one knows for oneself that the time has come; the body is free from the suffering of illness, the mind is without greedy attachment, and there is no delusion—just as if entering a state of meditative concentration.
The Buddha and the assembly of sages shall come to welcome me, holding a golden platform in their hands. In a single thought-moment, I shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;

as the lotus flower opens, I shall behold the Buddha, immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, and suddenly awaken to the Buddha-wisdom. There, I shall extensively deliver sentient beings and fulfill my vow for Bodhi.
With utmost sincerity, you must single-mindedly take refuge. Throughout your entire life, practice true cultivation by reciting the Buddha’s name.

At the time of making your vow, be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts, as if facing execution, being in prison, being pursued by enemies, or being threatened by water or fire. One...
With a heart seeking salvation, I vow to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly realize non-arising, and extensively deliver all sentient beings.
May I perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem and pledge to repay the four debts of gratitude. Only through such ultimate sincerity shall this not be in vain.

If, however, my words and deeds do not accord, if my faith and vows are slight, if there is no continuous succession of mindfulness, or if there are frequent interruptions—then due to such indolence, to hope for rebirth at the moment of death is merely...
I fear that one may be obstructed by karmic hindrances, fail to encounter virtuous friends, and be so oppressed by the winds and fires [of death] that right mindfulness cannot be established.
Why is this? Because the present moment is the cause and the time of death is the fruit; the cause must be real, for then the fruit will not be in vain.
The Buddha Vajradhvaja said: "All sentient beings should make a vow to be born in that land.

It would not exclude even those with female organs or physical deficiencies, nor those who have committed the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, or those bound for the Avīci Hell—how much less so me? Although my own practice of the Way is now slight,"

If one does not commit the five heinous crimes and recites the name ten times or more, one will certainly attain rebirth there. How could the Buddha deceive himself by contravening his own original vow?
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest the mark of the broad and long tongue to testify to this matter.
Therefore, I shall now resolutely seek rebirth there and dare not regress. This is called the adamantine banner-like power of the courageous practitioner.
Throughout one's life,
when one’s karmic affinity is joined through a pure mind, firm and steadfast faith, sincere worship and recitation, repentance, and the making of vows,
I know that this person— whether in body or mind— is joined with Amitābha in affinity, like a wind blowing upon a tree.

When a tree leans toward the west, at the time it falls, it will necessarily fall toward the west. It is exactly the same with those who practice goodness and attain birth [in the Pure Land]: they will certainly receive the guidance and reception [of the Buddha].

Most people in the world who recite the Buddha’s name do so merely for the sake of their fields of merit, for the sake of their kinsmen, or to seek recovery from the suffering of illness, as well as for eternal...

Because of this, people often offer incense and candles at places of practice, making vows that seek only worldly conditions—such as preserving wealth, status, and peace, or ensuring that their descendants will be illustrious.
Such aspirations are utterly contrary to the fundamental vow of Amitābha’s guidance.
Even if one practices for a lifetime with such misplaced effort, what benefit would there be? One should instead give rise to the genuine aspiration to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
Having personally received the prediction of enlightenment, one returns to the Sahā world to extensively deliver sentient beings, seeking not even a hair’s breadth of personal gain.

Making such vows for the blessings and rewards of humans and devas, one directs one's attention toward them at all times, rejoicing in them without forgetting; only then does one accord with the vow of the Buddha.
At the moment of death, one will certainly receive the guidance of the Buddhas to be reborn in their presence.
In the end, there were those who developed true faith in the Pure Land and resolved to be reborn there;

regardless of whether they had attained awakening or not, even those who followed the Single Transmission of Direct Pointing and had not yet awakened, though they made it their daily task to practice Chan meditation, were not hindered from making the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land. This is because...
One has not yet been able to transcend future existence; since there is still ultimately a place of birth, this is not yet the mind of theft or the mind of divergent paths.
Regarding those who have already attained awakening, the ancients said: "Do you think that with a single awakening you can immediately rank as equal to all Buddhas?
Thus, although every atom contains the Flower Treasury and every location is a Lotus Land, the Chapter on Conduct and Vows (Caryāpraṇidhāna) [remains essential].

It is surely with earnest devotion that one speaks of being reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. If this is so even for those who have already attained awakening, how much more so for those who have not?

It is certain that among worldly people, those who recite the Buddha’s name are many, while those who achieve Buddhahood are few. There are three reasons for this: first, although they recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths...

If one harbors unwholesome thoughts in the heart, one will not attain rebirth there. Therefore, one must rely on what the Buddha has taught: accumulate virtue and cultivate merit; be filial and obedient toward one's parents;
serve one's sovereign with loyalty; love one's brothers; respect one's spouse; and maintain utmost sincerity, faithfulness, and honesty.
Be gentle and patient; be impartial and upright; employ hidden and skillful means; have compassion for all beings. Do not kill living creatures;
do not insult those of low station; do not oppress the common people. Whenever an unwholesome thought arises, apply yourself with diligent mindfulness to counteract it.

One must certainly resolve to recite [the Buddha’s name] without retreat. This is not a good state of mind. Second, although one may recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth, if the mind harbors random thoughts and distractions, one will not attain rebirth there.
One must remain steadfast; even as the "monkey of the mind" and the "horse of the will" run wild, every syllable must be distinct and every thought closely monitored.
It should be as if one were personally in the Western Land, facing Amitābha, not daring to be distracted. Only in this way is it correct. Third.
Though such a person may recite the Buddha’s name with their mouth, in their heart they only wish not to lose their human form in future lives and seek wealth and status.
Because of this, they cannot attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, even the wealth and nobility of celestial palaces must end in a fall once one's merit is exhausted;
how much more so for the human realm? How long can it last? Therefore, one should immediately give rise to a vast mind, establish a firm resolve, and vow to attain rebirth. Upon seeing...
The Buddha heard the Dharma, attained the unsurpassed fruit, and extensively delivered sentient beings; only such a person as this is truly one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
They will certainly attain Buddhahood and never again fall back.
If one does not aspire to be born in the Pure Land, that is one thing; but if one aspires to be born there, then there is no way one will not be born.

It may be that one is not born in the Pure Land, but once born, there shall never be any falling back. An ordinary person bound by all fetters relies initially upon faith and aspiration to attain birth in that land;
yet, the three poisons and false views have not yet been suddenly forgotten. How, then, can it be known that they do not fall back? It is simply because of the power of Amitābha’s vows.
It is constantly sustained and maintained; its great radiance perpetually illuminates the assembly of superior beings. Their lifespan lasts for eternal kalpas.

The waterfowl, the groves of trees, and the sounds of the wind all resonate with the music of the sublime vehicle. Those who hear these sounds give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, and recollects the Sangha.
This is because there has never been an interruption [in this practice]. Sentient beings are like those afflicted by illness;

the Buddha is the King of Physicians, the Dharma is the excellent medicine, and the Sangha are the attendants who care for the sick. When these three are present before one, the illness cannot arise. It is for this reason that it is said:
Then one will be reborn in the Pure Land in this very life; how could there be any falling back?
Since his youth, Qian Nian-diao had sought a wife and raised children, managing the household affairs and enduring myriad hardships, until suddenly—
When the three-inch breath is severed, one cannot avoid having everything come to rest in a single morning. If one is a filial descendant, they can still remember their parents;
if one is an unworthy son, even while the parents have only just died and their bones are not yet cold, they squander the family property and indulge in pleasure as they please.
Judging by this, what is so important about it? It is but a thousand-year-old trick; descendants will take care of themselves.
This is the blessing for one's descendants. Do not become a "horse or ox" for your children and grandchildren. Since how much time can one have while living in this world?
Before falling ill and before growing old, shake off the concerns of body and mind and set aside worldly affairs. If you gain even a single day of time, recite the name of Amitābha for that day;
if you gain a single period of effort, cultivate pure karma for that period. Then, when the end of life arrives, it will be well.
I loathe death and dread it. My provisions for the journey have been prepared in advance; my path ahead has been made secure and steady.
Were it not so, repentance would be difficult to pursue.
The good news is that by relying on a single Buddha, with the mind following the mind without interruption, and practicing for a long time, one may then— with a single punch—
shatter this body composed of the four elements, and with a single kick, overturn this world composed of the five turbidities. Thereafter, according to one's...

Hearing birdsong and the chirping of cicadas, or listening to the songs of herdsmen and the chants of woodcutters—these are the sounds of the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, as well as the celestial music of the Western Paradise.
Bamboo fences and thatched huts are the golden terraces and jeweled palaces of the Western Paradise. Flying springs and babbling brooks...
The precious ponds and waters of virtue in the Western Land; the wild flowers and noble trees are the jeweled nets interlacing there;

the rain of wondrous blossoms from heaven; and the assembly of enlightened teachers and virtuous friends, as well as the companionship with wood, stone, deer, and boars—these are the various superior and good people of the West.
What suffering and what joy? What compliance and what opposition? What demons and what obstacles? What are the three?
Poisons and other afflictions are right before one's eyes, yet it is entirely a pure land. When the time comes to grow weary of the world, there is no fear and no confusion;
neither supporting nor maintaining a self, one stands with hands folded in serene composure, returning to one’s native home. This is entirely where one has gained strength throughout one’s life.
Reaching this point, you will certainly find it useful; indeed, there is good news.
Apart from the mind, there is no substance;
it is like the requirement for the ten recitations to be accomplished at the moment of death. One should simply prepare the bridge in advance by gathering merits and dedicating them.

If, at that time, every thought remains unimpaired, then one need have no anxiety. Indeed, the two wheels of good and evil and the two retributions of suffering and joy are all [dependent upon] the three...

It is created by karma, produced by the four conditions, accomplished by the six causes, and subsumed within the five fruits. If, for even a single moment of mind, one harbors anger or engages in sexual misconduct, this is the karma of hell.
If one is stingy, greedy, or untruthful, this is the karma of hungry ghosts. If one is obscured by ignorance and delusion, this is the karma of animals.
If one is arrogant and conceited, this is the karma of asuras. If one firmly upholds the five precepts, this is the karma of humans. If one practices with diligence...

The ten wholesome actions are the karma of the devas. Realizing the emptiness of persons is the karma of the śrāvakas. Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached is the karma of the pratyekabuddhas.
Cultivating the six perfections in equal measure is the karma of the bodhisattvas. True compassion and equanimity are the karma of the Buddhas.

If the mind is pure, one will be born through transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees; if the mind is defiled, one will receive birth in a foul land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines. All of these...
These are the fruits of such categories [of causes], capable of evoking superior conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Therefore, apart from the source of one’s own mind, there is no separate essence.

As a sutra says: "When the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; when the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure. It further states: "If you wish to purify your realm, simply purify your own mind.
Thus we know that all things return to the mind and the myriad dharmas arise from the self. If you wish to attain a pure fruit, simply...
Practice the pure cause. Just as the nature of water is to flow downward and the nature of fire is to rise upward, such is the force of their inherent tendencies; what room is there for doubt?

When the time of death arrives, you must remain fully mindful. What could possibly prevent it from manifesting? If you say that worldly concerns cannot be let go of, [then you have not yet understood].
If you say it is because you cannot let go of this body, I fear you will not be able to leap clear of it;

you will inevitably come back again. Why such attachment to it? If you say it is because you cannot sever this mind, I fear you will not be able to cut it off entirely, leaving it as a seed for future rebirth. Why such cherishing of it?

That is even more so. If you say that the Buddha-dharma cannot be set aside, it is likely because you have not yet opened up; you cling to it and thus create a bond of dharma. Furthermore, your need to cherish it is even more so.

If you worry about losing your faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*), then that very faculty of wisdom you recognize is precisely the life-root (*jīvitendriya*), and it is precisely the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭavijñāna*).
That single thought which fears being lost is precisely the grasping at self of the seventh consciousness (*saptavijñāna*). This is the division.
Separate yourself from the six consciousnesses; you must cast them off completely and utterly. Yet, the need to maintain mindfulness is even more critical.
As for the fundamentally pure, originally luminous, and wondrously enlightened nature, it admits no discrimination and requires no support.

Only when nothing at all is seen and not a single dharma remains can it manifest in its entirety. You have carried this delusion with you since time immemorial, and thus such a variety of things have come forth.

Today you have attained awakening; yet, do you still intend to take even a single thing with you? When you are utterly naked, without a single thread of attachment, only then will you realize the highest grade.
This is what is called "attaining that which accords with one's intent."
When an ordinary person’s life comes to an end and they wish to be reborn in the Pure Land, they must first make preparations; they must not fear death.

They should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering and entangled by evil karma. If one can cast off this defiled body and be reborn transcendentally in the Pure Land, one will behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
One will experience immeasurable happiness and attain great liberation; this is precisely what accords with one's wishes. It is like casting off tattered rags to put on precious garments.
You should simply let go of body and mind and harbor no attachment; wait for death with a single-minded focus.

Instruct your family members and those who come to visit and inquire after you: whenever anyone comes before me, have them recite the Buddha’s name for my sake, and do not speak of worldly matters at hand.
One must not engage in idle chatter regarding the family's affairs, whether good or bad, nor should one offer words of soft consolation or prayers for peace and well-being;

all such things are empty and of no benefit. If the illness is grave and death is imminent, relatives must not shed tears or wail, nor utter sounds of lamentation and distress, which will disturb the mind and cause the loss of right mindfulness. Instead, they should at that moment recite the Buddha’s name with one voice in unison.
One may only express grief once the breath has ceased. Should there be even the slightest attachment to this world, it will immediately become an obstacle, preventing liberation.
If one meets those who clearly understand the Pure Land and frequently comes to exhort and encourage them, it is a matter of the greatest fortune.
Those who rely upon this will certainly transcend this life to be reborn there; of this there is no doubt.

Regarding the sounding of the chime: whenever one encounters a member of one’s family or any other person approaching the end of life, first place a standing image of the Buddha in the bedroom before the bed, facing east.
The patient should face west, opposite the Buddha. Those attending the patient should burn incense, scatter flowers, and sound the chime.
One should assist in reciting the Buddha’s name. Even if the patient previously did not believe in the Buddha, one must employ various skillful means to exhort them to recite it.
If there are bodily discharges or impurities resulting from the illness, they should be removed immediately; this carries no fault, for the Buddha’s mind is compassionate.
I merely hope for their sincere return; I harbor no particular hatred or malice.

The Great Way of equality is dispassionate, treating enemies and kin with equal impartiality. However, the speech of ordinary people regarding attachment to their kinsmen may appear similar to this [equality].

This is not yet in accord with the truth. For those who do not realize that their passions and attachments have not yet been forgotten, there is only the cultivation of pure karma and the forming of companions for the Western Land.
Thus, their emotions return to the state beyond emotion, and their attachments become identical to the forgetting of attachment.

Without destroying the ordinary mind’s characteristics, they nonetheless universally attain rebirth; surely this is never anything less than impartial. This stands in contrast to those who, at the brink of peril, shed tears and bid farewell.
It is different. When one awaits a body that is about to decay, how can the magnitude of the affection be measured by those who exhaust their resources to provide a lavish funeral?

One who wishes to accomplish great matters with the "South-Pointing Chariot" must realize that the most critical point lies in the decisive move at the moment of need. To have been negligent in the past and to merely procrastinate until this point is of no avail.
One may not do so. What was previously a state of deluded attachment cannot be muddled here; what was previously superficial and ornate cannot be borrowed or feigned here;
what was previously a forked path cannot be wandered upon here. Within this very square inch, the numinous clarity takes charge.

If one awakens, the lotus pedestal immediately appears; if one remains in ignorance, there are the six paths and three realms of suffering, with their distinct divisions of purity and defilement—separate ways in an instant.
Alas! Ultimately, the essential key to be grasped does not lie outside these four characters: "One Mind, Right Mindfulness. At this moment, it is like drawing a bow to its full extent;

when the string is about to snap, it is exceedingly difficult to open. One must apply focused effort and maintain firm stability, letting go of the front hand while severing the connection to the back hand.
It is like being struck by an arrow; or like crossing the sea relying on a south-pointing chariot, so as not to err regarding one's direction.

As you are about to reach the other shore, you must urgently and carefully lower the sails and take hold of the rudder. If you miss the mark for even a moment, you will once again be blown away by a violent gale, drifting aimlessly upon the vast ocean—how then can you find a place of rest?

When returning to one's native land, the mind fundamentally does not arise; it arises only through the convergence of conditions. The mind fundamentally does not die; it dies only when conditions disperse.

Thus, while there appears to be birth and death, in reality there is no coming or going. If one realizes this, life will be harmonious and death peaceful; one will be eternally tranquil and eternally luminous. Worldly people fear death.
This is because one has not yet awakened to the fact that, from the very beginning, there is no arising. Since there is fundamentally no arising, how could there be death?
What, then, is there to fear? However, this non-arising is not easily realized all at once; one must simply practice mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded sincerity.

When such mindfulness is sustained for a long time until the mind is undistracted, awakening will surely be attained. Even if awakening is not reached, the power of a lifetime of mindfulness will be self-evident at the moment of death.
To die and be reborn in the Pure Land is like being adrift in a foreign land and finally returning to one's hometown.
Amitābha Buddha extends his hand to welcome and lead one to rebirth; with immeasurable joy, what is there to fear?

The auspicious signs are manifold when one attains the perfection of samādhi. Devas and humans provide protection and assistance; at the time of death, one maintains right mindfulness. At the moment of rebirth in the Pure Land, the auspicious signs are manifold:
sometimes celestial music fills the sky, sometimes extraordinary fragrances pervade the chamber, sometimes light illuminates the body, or [jewels...]
The seat appears before them; or Amitābha extends his arm to personally welcome them; or a Bodhisattva holds out a platform, taking their hand to receive them.

Even when they know in advance that the time has arrived, their right mindfulness remains unerring. All obstacles suddenly vanish into emptiness, and they are naturally able to bathe themselves and sit in the full lotus posture.
They gather the assembly to preach the Dharma, join their palms in farewell, or further exhort others to advance on the Path. They may write verses, cast down their pens, and pass away.
They pass away while holding [the object] in their palms. Or, after death, their entire bodies remain as if alive;

their teeth, bones, and rosaries do not burn when set on fire, and their flames are extraordinary, vividly manifesting in five colors. Auspicious objects hover and swirl in the air without dispersing, and wherever the smoke reaches, [miracles occur].
The flowing pearls of śarīra arise upon contact with objects; these are things commonly seen and heard of.
Were it not for the power of diligent practice, clarity, and spiritual progress cultivated over many days, how could such a thing be possible?

For an amulet to travel a hundred *li*, one must grind grain overnight; for a thousand *li*, one must gather provisions for three months. How much more so for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, spanning ten trillion *kṣetras*!
If one does not prepare in advance during one’s lifetime, yet hopes to seize it in a mere instant, I do not know what storehouse one will find.
When Your Majesty breathes, can you possess the skill of Zhuge Liang watching the fish or Anshi playing chess? Can you overcome a great adversary?
Regarding the words that even a base person may attain rebirth through ten recitations, one need not narrow one’s perspective too tightly;

for while the principles of the sutras are certainly trustworthy, they were also the desperate, compassionate words of the Tathāgata when there was no other recourse, and should not be treated as mere convenience.

I have now prepared these protective talismans for such people as you. Furthermore, it is truly pitiable that while human nature generally favors excellence and loathes inferiority, you alone are content to consider yourselves the very lowest in this particular matter.

Third, regarding the doubts of those who practice nianfo at the time of death: there are three doubts that one must not fail to heed. First, the doubt: "My karmic obstacles from past lives are heavy and my cultivation has been shallow for only a few days;
I fear I shall not attain rebirth. Second, the doubt: "I have unfinished aspirations and my greed, anger, and ignorance have not yet ceased; I fear..."
One must not give rise to three doubts. These are: "Although I have been mindful of the Buddha, I fear that at the time of my death he will not come to welcome me.
Because of these three doubts, they become obstacles; one loses right mindfulness and fails to attain rebirth there. Now, through three explanations, these three doubts shall be dispelled.
First: "Karma is fundamentally illusory; when the mind is pure, it is empty. One need not doubt that heavy karma [prevents rebirth]. Second: [The second point is:]...

Sentient emotions are like dreams and illusions; once awakened, what remains? If you naturally consent to cease the machinations of the mind, greed and anger will be severed accordingly. Do not doubt this. Third:
When practice is focused and mindfulness is earnest, the Buddha appears within your own mind. The Buddha does not come from elsewhere. Do not doubt this.

Regarding the four obstacles: although ordinary persons may possess faith and practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, if their karmic obstructions from past lives are heavy, they cannot escape the suffering of illness.

If, because of this, they achieve repentance and awakening, surrendering body and mind with sincerity to take refuge in the Buddha, they will naturally be reborn in the Pure Land. As for those without wisdom, their resolve for the Way is not firm.
Yet they say, "I am now reciting the Buddha's name, yet I suffer from illness; this is a slander against Amitābha. By this single thought, they enter directly into hell—this is the first barrier.

Or, while in daily life they speak of the Pure Land with their mouths but cherish the *saṃsāra* world in their hearts, they fail to plant roots of transcendental goodness and seek only worldly benefits.
When facing death and encountering illness, they fear dying and crave life, blindly trusting shamans and sorcerers.

To take life; to pray to gods and spirits; because of these, the mind becomes deviant, one lacks the protection of the Buddha, and wanders through the three miserable realms—this is the second barrier.
To observe the fasts and precepts, yet due to taking medicine, or being pressured by others, to break the precepts and consume pungent foods:
such a person lacks resolute faith and loses their roots of goodness—this is the third barrier. At the time of death, to fix one's thoughts on family wealth and property, and to be attached to...

One becomes attached to kinsmen and family; unable to let go of them in one's heart, one loses right mindfulness and consequently falls into the realm of hungry ghosts or is reborn as an insect or beast, guarding one’s household as if it were one’s own birthday.
This is the fourth barrier. Thus, Inspector Yang said: "If love is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha;
if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in the Pure Land. Truly, these words are true. Those who cultivate the practice of the Pure Land must...
In ordinary times, investigate thoroughly; at the critical moment, ensure there is no confusion. Let go of everything completely and keep Amitābha in every thought.
If you can maintain this single thought with steadfastness, you will be able to shatter those four barriers.

Regarding the "one who attains rebirth through seven parts," namely the one who attains rebirth through ten recitations: this refers to reciting ten times oneself during one's lifetime, not requesting another person to recite after death.
As for reciting oneself during one's lifetime, at the moment of the end of life, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas will personally come to welcome one; therefore, it is essential.
As for being reborn in the Pure Land, it is uncertain whether one will have others recite [the scriptures] on one's behalf after death. As the Sūtra says:
"If others perform religious services for one after death, one receives only one-seventh of the merit; if one performs them oneself while alive, one receives a thousand- or ten-thousandfold reward."

One must not harbor the thought that it is permissible to commit evil throughout one's life and then recite the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, hoping for rebirth while still burdened by one's karma;

such a thing occurs only when one possesses the karmic conditions of past roots of goodness and merit, thereby meeting a spiritual teacher who can exhort one to recite the Buddha’s name. Such fortunate circumstances occur but once in ten thousand cases. If one were to...
When one is on the verge of death, the "wind-swords" dismember the body, the four elements separate, and one is oppressed by manifold sufferings;

in such frantic terror and agitation, one is unable to recite the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, even if you die while free from illness, it may still be that your worldly affairs are not yet concluded or your worldly attachments have not ceased.
Clinging to life and fearing death, the chest is agitated and disturbed. If one is a worldly person, this is compounded by private family affairs;
having not clarified what lies beyond, and with the wailing of wife and children yet unprepared for, one is scorched by a hundred kinds of anxieties and cannot recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even before death, when there is but a slight illness upon the body, one must endure pain and suffering, crying out and groaning, asking for medicine and seeking [relief].
Furthermore, when you are ill, you pray, offer sacrifices, and repent; your miscellaneous thoughts fly about in confusion, and you are unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Even setting aside the time before you were ill, you are simply advanced in years, with signs of decay appearing before you;

exhausted and decrepit, filled with lamentation, grief, and distress, you merely arrange your affairs on the left and right around this aging body, and thus cannot recite the Buddha’s name. Even setting aside the time before you grew old...
This is precisely the time of youth and vigor; it is the very moment one ought to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Should the wild mind falter even slightly, becoming entangled in worldly affairs, wandering east and west with distracted thoughts and delusions, and remaining lost in the vast expanse of karmic consciousness, one will be unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Furthermore, even if you possess leisure and independence and are determined to cultivate the path, if you cannot clearly discern through the phenomena of the world and fail to let go of them, you will be held fast by them.
It is uncertain; while sitting, one does not cease [distractions]. Suddenly, some slight object appears before one, and the single master follows after these delusions.

One cannot achieve mindfulness of the Buddha—just observe this! During times of old age and illness, or even on days of youth and leisure, if there is even the slightest matter occupying the mind, one already fails to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; how much more so when it comes to the time of death?

There are ten types of people who, despite having practiced their cultivation in advance, will be unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death: First, they may not necessarily encounter virtuous friends, and thus there will be no one to exhort them to mindfulness.
Second, they will be so entangled by the suffering of karma that they will have no leisure for mindfulness. Third, they may suffer from hemiplegia and lose [their faculties].
1. Speech: One cannot adequately praise the Buddha. 2. Madness and loss of mind: Focused contemplation is difficult to achieve.
3. Encountering water or fire: There is no leisure for sincere devotion. 4. Encountering tigers or wolves: One is startled and in a state of haste.
5. At the point of death, evil friends: They destroy and break one's faith. 6. Overeating to excess: One falls into a stupor and dies. 7. Battlefields and combat: [One is distracted by conflict.]

1. Those who are cruel and violent perish in an instant. 10. Those who suddenly fall from high cliffs lose their lives and ruin their nature. These ten kinds of people will, at the moment of death, certainly be unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
They must practice in advance so that their pure karma is accomplished; even if they encounter difficult circumstances, [they will be saved].
One will certainly receive the Buddha’s protection.

When the bandits have departed, one may close the gates and seek medical treatment to take medicine; this will not initially cause any hindrance. However, while medicine can treat illness, it cannot preserve life. One must instead pray to the deities for blessings.
This merely increases one’s karmic offenses. When life comes to its end, what can these minor ghosts do? To be filled with empty panic is of no avail to anyone.

Only when the breath has faded and life is spent, and consciousness has entered the realm of darkness, will you begin to recite the ten invocations and strike the bell—just like closing the gate after the thief has fled;
what benefit does this accomplish? The matter at the door of death is momentous; it requires that you exert effort yourself before it is possible. If [you wait until] one...
If one’s mindfulness falters, one will suffer through kalpas; who can take one’s place? Reflect on this, reflect on it!
By chanting even a single sound for the duration of a cow chewing its cud, sins as numerous as grains of sand are extinguished.
By perfecting ten recitations, one’s form shall dwell in the Pure Land, rescuing those in peril and uprooting those in distress.

Rare obstacles are eliminated and grievances are resolved; it is not merely that one is temporarily pulled from the ford of suffering for a single lifetime. By relying on these causes and conditions, one ultimately casts oneself into the ocean of awakening. Thus the Sūtra says:
"If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and utters 'Namo Buddha' even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
It further says: "For example, suppose there is a person who, as soon as they are born and fall to the ground, is able to travel a thousand *li* in a single day. Their feet—
To fill a thousand years with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift to the Buddha is not equal to someone, in a future evil age, uttering the name of a single Buddha even once;

the latter’s merit surpasses the former. Furthermore, it is said that while the merit of providing the four requisites of support to all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa is immeasurable, if there are sentient beings who maintain a continuous flow of wholesome intention and recite the name of the Buddha even for the duration of a single grain of rice, [their merit is even greater].
The merit obtained [from this] is even more inconceivable than the former; there is no one who can measure it.

Regarding the comparison between suffering and happiness, a sutra states: "The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various joys; therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). Now, by means of...

Compare this with that [Sukhāvatī]. Here, one possesses a physical body of flesh and blood; all who are born here experience suffering. There, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower; there is no suffering of birth.
Here, the seasons change and pass, and the affliction of aging daily encroaches. There, cold and heat do not shift, and there is no suffering of aging.
Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize, and illnesses frequently arise. There, the body is a fragrant transformation-body...
In this world, there is purity, yet one suffers the pain of illness; such is rare even among those of seventy years. Impermanence is swift, and thus there is the suffering of death.
Therein, however, life spans are immeasurable, and thus there is no suffering of death. In this world, there are ties of kinship and affection; where there is love, there must be separation.

Therein, however, there are no parents, wives, or children, and thus there is no suffering of being separated from loved ones. In this world, there are enemies and vengeful foes; where there is enmity, there must be encounter. Therein, however, [there are none].

Those above gather in the assembly of supreme goodness; they have no association with the hateful or the resentful. Here, there is suffering from hunger and cold, and greed for more is never satisfied;
there, clothing, food, and precious treasures are provided for enjoyment as a matter of course. Here, the physical form is coarse and ugly, and the six sense faculties are often deficient;
there, the appearance is dignified and majestic, and the body possesses radiance. Here, one revolves through birth and death; there, one eternally realizes the Unconditioned.
In this world, there are the sufferings of the four realms of rebirth; in that world, even the names of the three evil paths do not exist.
Here, there are thorns, pits, and ravines, with high and low ground that is uneven, filled with earth, stones, sand, and silt, and defiled by impurities.

There, the ground is made of gold, jewel-trees reach toward the heavens, towers soar with the seven precious gems, and flowers of four colors bloom. Here, the twin śāla trees have already withered, and the Dragon Flower tree has yet to appear; there—

In this case, the Honored One of Immeasurable Life is currently preaching the Dharma; there, one merely gazes up at the auspicious names of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, whereas there, one personally has these two superior beings as one’s most excellent friends.
In this case, various demons and non-Buddhists disturb and confuse one’s correct cultivation;
there, the Buddha’s transformation is unified, and the traces of demons and non-Buddhists are severed. In this case, seductive forms and licentiousness delude the practitioner; there...
Thus, their primary retribution is pure; in reality, there are no women there. Here, malevolent beasts and *chi-mei* spirits clamor with perverse sounds;
there, waterfowl and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. When comparing these two lands, the conditions of their environments are vastly different.
This should inspire the people of this world with great delight; would they not look toward the Land of Bliss and leap for joy?
There is nothing that is not for the purpose of skillfully seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Although this is a matter concerning the time after death, it is of great benefit during one's life.

For the Buddha’s teaching of people is nothing other than goodness; since one has made the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land one’s heart-mind, whatever is conceived by the will and uttered by the mouth—
As for what has been said: whatever the body does, there is nothing that is not good. In this present life, one may thus become a gentleman;

people will respect him and the spirits will assist him. His fortune and rank may increase, and his lifespan may be prolonged. However, he may subsequently be deprived of these by the conditions of his karma.
Although one may not be able to devote oneself single-mindedly to this, evil conditions will be diminished by it, and wholesome conditions will increase from it.
Next, there are those who do not understand where propriety and righteousness lie; they fear only punishments and esteem only physical strength, pursuing power and profit.
If even such persons take the Pure Land as their goal, they will surely examine themselves and reproach their own conduct. Although—
If one can bring all actions into accord with ritual propriety and righteousness, how could they ever again fall into sin or punishment?

Since you have already attained verification through study and focused cultivation, you ought to seek spiritual efficacy. Today, your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; the signs of death are manifest before you. Know this!
When the end of one's life approaches, how many days remain? One must face it directly; one must simply wish to see the Buddha.
For instance, Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu was blessed by the Buddha’s hand upon his head three times throughout his lifetime. Furthermore, Master Huigan recited the Buddha’s name with such devotion.
One will then immediately behold the Buddha. When Dharma Master Shaokang chanted "Buddha" once, the assembly saw a Buddha fly out from his mouth;
when he chanted "Buddha" a hundred times, it was likewise so, appearing like a string of pearls. Such miraculous responses have occurred tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of times.
If your mind remains uninterrupted, it is not difficult to see the Buddha; if an interrupted thought arises, you will certainly not see the Buddha, for you will lack the karmic affinity with him.
It is difficult to be born in the Pure Land; if one is not born in the Pure Land, one will inevitably fall into the evil realms.
Thus, even a single moment of a distracted mind constitutes the karma for the three miserable paths and the evil realms. Beware! Beware!

To distance oneself from Māra, there is only this Dharma-gate. By relying on the power of the Buddha, if one practices it, success is certain; there will be no further demonic activities, and one shall never again regress.
Not only does it distance one from Māra, but it also [protects against] all human officials, verbal disputes, matters of right and wrong, calamities and hardships, as well as water and fire.
Robbers, evil persons, and calamitous events—even tigers, wolves, insects, and beasts, as well as ghosts, specters, and malevolent spirits—cannot cause harm.
Furthermore, one shall not be afflicted by any epidemics, dysentery, fevers, abscesses, scabies, or ailments of the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue.
Provided that one’s vows and practices remain unimpaired, all such misfortunes can be dispelled; however, [one may still be troubled] by fame, gain, and the sweetness of affection.
The soft thief, as well as the fire of greed born of anger—though the power of the Buddha exists, these are one's own faults and cannot be saved.

Regarding the sevenfold superior merits of mindfulness of the Buddha, there are seven kinds of superiority: first, the superiority of having few words and being easy to practice, consisting of the single phrase "Namo A... [Amitābha].
1. It is superior because Amitābha Buddha is worthy of being contemplated by all people. 2. It is superior because the object of the second contemplation—the Buddha’s realm—is sublime;

with a single mind, one contemplates the Buddha’s body, its marks and signs, and takes the Pure Land as the object. 3. It is superior because it brings liberation from calamities and the attainment of peace;

the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, so that they are free from all afflictions and sufferings, and enjoy tranquility, celebration, and auspiciousness. 4. It is superior because reciting the name extinguishes transgressions; a single [recitation] of mindfulness of the Buddha...
1. Regarding sound: A single utterance extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. 2. Regarding the merit of recitation:
To recite the Buddha’s name once is superior to offering the seven treasures of the four continents to the Buddhas and Arhats. 3. Regarding the result of seeing the Buddha:

Sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly see the Buddha. 4. Regarding the excellence of being welcomed to rebirth: Transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emit light to welcome them.

When a practitioner is reborn in the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name with a loud voice possesses ten kinds of merit: first, it can dispel sleep; second, it causes the celestial Māras to be struck with terror; third...
1. The sound pervades the ten directions. 2. The sufferings of the three miserable realms are stilled. 3. External sounds do not enter. 4. The mind is made undistracted.
5. Courageous diligence arises. 6. All Buddhas rejoice. 7. Samādhi manifests before one. 8. One is reborn in the Pure Land.

Exhorting others to cultivate meritorious rewards means being able to encourage even a single person to practice the Pure Land. By virtue of these wholesome conditions, one can eliminate and dissolve transgressions,
increase and exalt blessings and longevity, offer posthumous offerings for deceased spirits, and adorn the Pure Land— how much more so when one encourages as many as five people!
If ten people further exhort one another, the Dharma-gift becomes vast and its meritorious retribution immeasurable. Thus, the verse for exhorting practice says:
"To encourage two others to practice is more meritorious than one's own diligence; when encouragement reaches ten or more people, the merit is already immeasurable."
One who encourages even a hundred or a thousand [to practice] is called a true Bodhisattva; one who can exceed ten thousand is Amitābha himself.

When prostrating to the Buddha, with each single bow, from the knees down to the adamantine foundation (vajra-tala), for every single mote of dust, one attains the rank of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
There are ten kinds of merit: first, obtaining an exquisite physical body; second, one’s words being trusted by others; third, being fearless when among the multitude;

fourth, being protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas; fifth, possessing great dignified deportment; sixth, being closely attached to by all people; seventh, being loved and respected by the devas; eighth, possessing great merit and virtue;
ninth, being reborn in a superior realm at the end of life; and tenth, swiftly realizing nirvāṇa.
The Buddha revealed the method for practicing in the Pure Land to remedy the ten failures of cultivation, so that all sentient beings may swiftly transcend birth and death.
However, those with heavy karmic obstructions who are unwilling to advance in their practice have ten kinds of failure: first, not believing the Buddha’s words; second, not following the sages...
[The ten faults are: first, not revering the Buddha; second, not honoring the Dharma; third, not believing in cause and effect; fourth, not valuing one’s own spiritual nature;

fifth, not seeking advancement; sixth, not associating with virtuous friends; seventh, not seeking liberation; eighth, willingly accepting saṃsāra; ninth, not fearing the evil realms; and tenth, willingly identifying with the ranks of Māra.
Those who practice by reversing these [faults] will obtain ten kinds of benefits.
Regarding the ten kinds of merit:
if a person upholds the name of even a single Buddha, they shall obtain these ten kinds of meritorious benefits in this present life.
First, throughout the day and night, the great powerful divine generals of the heavens, together with their retinues, will constantly protect them while remaining invisible. Second, the Emperor...
First, twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, as well as all bodhisattvas, will constantly follow and protect them.
Second, they will always be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas day and night; Amitābha Buddha will constantly emit light rays to gather in and sustain this person.
Third, no evil spirits, whether yakṣas or rākṣasas, will be able to harm them. Fourth, no venomous snakes [will be able to harm them].

1. No poisons whatsoever shall be able to take effect. 2. One shall not suffer from any of the five kinds of calamities involving fire, water, enemies, bandits, or weapons, nor from imprisonment, shackles, or untimely or unjust deaths.
3. All previously committed sins shall be completely extinguished. The lives of those one has killed as enemies shall all attain liberation, and there shall be no further retribution or opposition.
4. One’s dreams at night shall be upright; or else, one may dream of seeing the Buddha.

1. One will behold the supreme and wondrous form-body of Amitābha Buddha. 2. One’s eight consciousnesses will be constantly joyful; one’s complexion will be radiant and lustrous, and one’s vital energy will be full and flourishing.

3. Whatever one undertakes will be auspicious and successful. 4. One will always be respectfully honored, provided for, and prostrated to by all the people of the world, just as if they were honoring a Buddha.
5. At the time of death, one’s mind will be free from fear, right mindfulness will manifest before them, and one will behold Amitābha.
Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas and holy ones will hold golden platforms in their hands to welcome and guide them to rebirth in the Western Pure Land,
where they shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss until the end of the future.

The ten superior qualities of the Pure Land are as follows: First, one constantly beholds the Buddha; for since Amitāyus Buddha attained enlightenment, ten great kalpas have passed, and he remains eternally present without ceasing.
Second, one constantly hears the sound of the Dharma; for the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, the trees, the forests, the waters, and the birds perpetually proclaim the sublime Dharma.
Third, there is the assembly of the three sages and saints; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve as their supreme companions, for all these superior virtuous people gather in one place.
Fourth, there is the distancing from demonic activities; although there may be celestial Māras, they all protect the Buddha-dharma so that practitioners may swiftly achieve accomplishment.
Fifth, there is no undergoing of saṃsāra; through transformation-birth within a lotus flower, one no longer revolves through the painful realms of birth and death.
Therefore: Sixth, they are forever free from the evil realms; for in that Buddha-land, even the names of the three evil paths are not heard.
Seventh, there are superior conditions that assist the Path; jade towers, precious palaces, exquisite robes, and fine delicacies all serve as requisites to aid the Path.
Eighth, their lifespan is immeasurable; the life-span of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha, such that ordinary humans and devas exhaust their full term.
Regarding their power of wisdom: because its measure cannot be known; regarding those born into the assembly of those correctly established in the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*):

because they are all *avaivartika*, being non-retrogressive; regarding the fulfillment of the practices in eleven births: because they constantly follow the Buddha’s teachings; and regarding the attainment of unsurpassed *bodhi* in one birth: because it is attained in that single lifetime.
Regarding the ten ease-factors for rebirth:

first, because Amitābha’s vows are profound, rebirth is easy; second, because in Sukhāvatī there is no opposition, rebirth is easy; third, because all Buddhas of the ten directions provide protection, rebirth is easy;
fourth, because one Buddha from the east assists in its accomplishment, rebirth is easy; fifth, because the two great sages come to welcome the practitioner, rebirth is easy.

Sixth, it is easy to be led away by the eight great bodhisattvas. Seventh, it is easy to attain rebirth by practicing the ten vows. Eighth, it is easy to attain rebirth by transcribing a single sutra.
Ninth, it is easy to attain rebirth by dedicating scattered roots of goodness. Tenth, it is easy to attain rebirth by recollecting the Buddha for even a short time.

If the various precepts are not pure, and if the virtue of the precepts is not cultivated, upon what can one rely to establish one's practice? It is like one who wishes to store clarified butter (ghṛta) in a vessel and first cleanses away all impurities;
the practitioner of samādhi is likewise so. Only when the various precepts are pure can success be achieved. Even if one has residual karma from past lives...
Because they are deep-seated and cannot be severed instantaneously, one should likewise employ skillful means to restrain them.

One should exhort one's own mind to examine oneself and repent of transgressions, clearly understanding that worldly pleasures are few while sufferings are many, and that all things are impermanent, subject to decay, and will soon perish.
Realizing that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally impure, one should employ every possible expedient to ensure their definitive cessation.

Regarding the *Necklace of Jewels* (*Yingluo zhu*), one first receives the Three Refuges, next upholds the Five Precepts, and gradually cultivates the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas to perfect the threefold aggregate of discipline (*tri-saṃvara*).

When the faculties are mature, one maintains them in their entirety; when the faculties are not yet developed, one accepts them partially. There are three wholesome days in each month and six days of fasting (*upoṣadha*) in each month. Should it be as follows—

Regarding the five precepts: setting aside those that are difficult to practice, even the two flavors of wine and meat—which are among the ten grave offenses that are easy to transgress—one should at least uphold the single gate of non-killing.
As light dust accumulates into a mountain and falling dew adds to a river, so too does this practice grow. Thus, a sutra says: "While the Buddha is in the world, take the Buddha as your teacher;
after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, take the precepts as your teacher. It further states: "The precepts are like the bright sun and moon, and also like jeweled necklaces. Subtle...
The multitude of Bodhisattvas attained perfect enlightenment by this means. Now, seeing that they uphold the precepts and refrain from killing, they possess benevolence without seeking it;

seeing that they observe the precepts and refrain from stealing, they possess righteousness without aspiring for it; seeing that they spread the practice of refraining from sexual misconduct, they possess propriety without praying for it;

seeing that they establish themselves in refraining from falsehood, they possess faith without yearning for it; seeing that they exalt the practice of refraining from intoxicants, they possess wisdom without practicing it through mere intellect. It is clear that this is not merely...

To discipline oneself and guard against wrongdoing is also to assist the state in propagating its transformative teachings. Those who wish to cultivate pure conduct must strictly protect the roots of the precepts.

The Vinaya governs the mind to constitute the precepts; from the precepts arises meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and from concentration issues forth wisdom (*prajñā*). How great is the significance of the precepts! Thus said the Buddha.

The precepts are supremely subtle. Regarding the precept against killing, it extends even to the tiniest crawling insect; if one harbors even the slightest resentment or envy, the precept against killing becomes impure.

Regarding the eye perceiving forms and the ear perceiving sounds, the precept against stealing becomes impure. If one hears the sound of hairpins or bracelets through a wall, the precept against sexual misconduct becomes impure.
Reaching this level of refinement, body and mind are both severed, and both phenomena and principle are fully exhausted. Thus, one maintains the precepts amidst the conditions of worldly life.
How could one possibly discuss each case on the same footing as those who have merely received the tonsure and dyed robes? What is valued is the greatness of one's training of the mind;
one must exert effort at the fundamental point. Once one has attained sudden, liberating awakening, then even a cough, a sneeze, or a swinging of the arms will be nothing other than the pure Vinaya.

However, one must not claim attainment before it is attained and thereby give rise to a deluded understanding, asserting that drinking wine and eating meat do not obstruct bodhi, or that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder prajñā; such views lead only to falling into the realm of Māra.
If you can indeed reflect back upon yourself from time to time and maintain constant mindfulness at every moment, applying effort toward the original koan of "Buddha-mindfulness," then not only...
In the future there will be further enlightenment; even now, one may personally gain mastery. With a sovereign ruler over daily life, one does not turn along with external objects.
Even if one dwells in the arena of sound, form, fame, and profit, or is surrounded day and night by wife and kin, it does not hinder one from moving in harmony with the world.
Blending with the mundane and harmonizing with the light, one naturally emerges from defilement—mired in the mud yet unstained. This is what is meant by being "in the midst of dust."
This is the Great Gate of Liberation.

To realize that emotions—joy and anger, likes and dislikes, cravings and desires—are all merely emotional states is essential. To nourish these emotions leads to evil; to indulge them is to become a thief; to subdue them is [liberation].

Excellent. To extinguish the emotions is to be a sage. To find sweetness in one’s food and drink, beauty in one’s clothing, and spaciousness in one’s dwelling—such things as these constitute the nourishment of the emotions.
To have food and drink flowing like a stream, clothing that is entirely ornate, and dwellings where there is no satiety—such things as these constitute the indulgence of the emotions.
Not to calculate when offended, not to be angry when provoked, and not to harbor resentment when harmed—this is called "breaking" [the emotions].
When one encounters, touches, or harms others with passion, it is like [encountering] empty space; instead, one gives rise to a heart of compassion for their ignorance.
This is what is meant by "extinguishing passion. To realize this principle is for the mind-ground to be eternally pure, as if dwelling in a Pure Land.
Toward all sentient beings, whether enemies or kin, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, free from the notions of "other" and "self. Why is this so?

If one perceives an enemy as distinct from a relative, that is discrimination. Because of such discrimination, various forms of hatred and attachment arise; and due to these conditions of aversion and compliance, one creates [karmic actions].
All evil karmas ripen as such; therefore, one obtains bitter fruits. When others come with enmity, one must respond with intimacy.
Toward those who harbor poison, one should repay them with kindness. One should contemplate thus: "In the past I troubled you, and now you are angry with me.

This is due to my own past transgressions. Even if I were to lose my life for it, I should willingly accept it—how could I dare to be angry? Even if there were none [of such offenses] in previous lives..."
"Sinful! Now they treat me with resentment and hatred, even insolently insulting and overbearing me. I ought to reflect: Are they wise? Or are they ignorant?

If they are wise, they desire to bring my perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to fulfillment; they are my gracious teachers. How could I encounter them otherwise than by seeking to repay their kindness?
How would I dare harbor opposition? If they are ignorant, they are nonetheless a field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*), like a mother who hears..."
When the child returns the abuse, the mother’s heart only turns toward greater joy; she merely continues to caress him, never showing a trace of resentment.

Out of pity for his childish ignorance, she bestows only deep kindness upon him. Now it is just the same: he is besieged within by afflictions (*kleśa*), and the delusive Māra secretly employs him as an emissary.

His wild nature has not yet ceased, and his power is not his own. With this compassionate mind, one should only extend rescue and salvation; how could it be right to dwell on his faults? Thus one should reflect.
To regard them as enemies—if one gives rise to a contrary mind, how does this differ from ignorance? Those who desire to be strong rely on them to be strong;
those who desire to be high rely on them to be high. How could there be any opposition or compliance, or hatred and love, within them?
In this profound obscurity, if one gives rise to even a single improper thought, utters a single improper word, beholds a single improper form,

or hears a single improper sound, it is nothing but fault and evil; how much more so for that which is eaten— the flesh of sentient beings— and that which is worn— also obtained by killing sentient beings.

This is already so; how much more so regarding all other transgressions and evils? These do not stop at the consumption of meat or the wearing of silk. One might simply not think of them, but once one does think of them, they are truly terrifying.
From youth to old age, from birth until death, as these accumulations become numerous, they become entangling and solid, leaving no way for liberation.
After closing one's eyes [in death], one cannot avoid departing according to the conditions of one's karma, into a realm of profound obscurity and darkness—how can one know [what awaits]?
In what place are we adrift and submerged, with no time of emergence in sight? Only the Western Pure Land serves as the most direct shortcut for transcending saṃsāra.
A physical body is difficult to obtain; while you possess good health, attend to this great matter.
Seventh, do not leave the home life for the sake of birth and death as if it were your true purpose; rather, desire to accomplish your liberation in this single lifetime.
From time to time, admonish yourself with these seven matters and strive diligently to maintain them. First, do not accumulate wealth, build houses, purchase fields, or acquire any refined luxuries.

Regarding fine objects—such as scriptures and images—that have been transmitted from antiquity and originate from renowned families: do not harbor any lingering attachment to them. Maintain single-minded right mindfulness.

Second, you must not engage in various non-essential matters that obstruct meritorious conditions; wait until another day when the Great Matter has been clarified, for it will not be too late to do so then.
For now, temporarily set aside the gateway of myriad practices and maintain single-minded right mindfulness. Third, you must not...
One gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward beautiful forms, delicious tastes, and the like; one gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward pleasant words that praise me.
One does not give rise to a mind of anger or vexation toward ugly forms, unpleasant tastes, and the like, nor toward harsh words that revile me.
When others revile me or treat me with various forms of opposition, I shall give rise to no heart of anger or affliction.
Regarding matters of the past or future, whether favorable or adverse, I shall completely set them aside and maintain firm resolve and steadfast defense.

With single-minded right mindfulness, I must not compose poetry or prose, nor engage in calligraphy—whether in regular, running, or cursive scripts—nor write inscriptions, couplets, or ornate letters, nor peruse external secular texts.
Do not engage in debate with others regarding their gains and losses, strengths and weaknesses, or even instruct them based on mere personal opinions while harboring a haughty mind in your writings.
Do not, while your meditation has not yet reached full realization, recklessly attempt to critique or evaluate it. Maintain a sealed mouth and a tongue at rest, keeping the mind in right mindfulness.

Fifth, do not associate with friends or relatives, nor respond to invitations, travel to mountains to enjoy the scenery, or engage in miscellaneous talk and idle chatter—none of these various worldly matters.
Settle matters of principle within yourself. Regarding what must be decided and cannot be postponed, attend to it; all else shall be suspended.

With single-minded right mindfulness, do not for a moment indulge in greed, attachment, negligence, or excessive sleep. Until the Great Matter is clarified, endure toil and suffering with single-minded right mindfulness.
Seventh, do not compete with worldly people over talent or ability, nor strive for fame or power. Do not speak of what you have not yet attained...
To claim attainment when one has not yet realized it, to deceive by professing oneself a "knower," and to falsely exalt oneself—these are improper.

One should instead maintain humility and preserve one's state of ignorance, remaining throughout life on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*). Therein, one should refine oneself, always being diligent and ever-striving, with single-minded right mindfulness.
In releasing living beings, everyone loves their own life; every creature craves survival. How can one slaughter their bodies to satisfy one's own appetite?

Whether by cutting open their bellies with sharp blades, piercing their hearts with pointed knives, flaying their skin or scraping off their scales, severing their throats or splitting their shells, or boiling them...
Boiling turtles and eels alive; or salt-pickling crabs and shrimp raw—how pitiable! They suffer great agony with no means of escape, enduring extreme pain that is hard to bear.
Having committed such sky-reaching evil karma, they bind themselves in enmity for ten thousand generations. When the day of impermanence arrives, they immediately fall into hell:
into boiling cauldrons and glowing coals, amidst sword-trees and knife-mountains. When their punishment is exhausted, they are reborn as animals once more—a cycle of endless resentment.
As for retribution: when one's life ends, it will be repaid in kind. Once the debt is settled and one returns to human form, one will suffer many illnesses and a premature death;

one may die by the hands of snakes or tigers, or die by the blade of war, or die by official punishment, or die by poison—all of which are the karmic results induced by killing. I inform all people of the world:

I do not dare compel you to observe the fast, but I first urge you to refrain from killing. To those households that refrain from killing, virtuous deities shall provide protection, and calamities [shall not arise].
Transverse obstacles will be eliminated. Your lifespan shall be long and enduring; your descendants shall be virtuous and filial; and various forms of auspiciousness will be beyond full description.

If you can further release living beings according to your capacity and perform recitation of the Buddha’s name with empowerment, not only will your merit and virtue increase, but you will surely be reborn in accordance with your vows, forever escape the cycle of saṃsāra, and enter the stage of non-retrogression.
Refrain from killing the myriad creatures produced by Heaven and Earth to provide for human sustenance— such as various grains, various fruits, various vegetables,
and various delicacies from both water and land— and yet humans, through their clever ingenuity, further process them by baking, kneading, salting, acidifying, and boiling.
To roast them—this may indeed be called having a thousand feet and ten thousand feet [of satisfaction]. Why suffer by carrying them further?

They share the same vital breath, the same mother-and-child bond, and the same capacity for perception; they feel pain and itchiness, and they experience birth and death. To kill and eat such creatures—is this not contrary to reason?
It is commonly said that it only matters that the heart be good, and that one need not observe vegetarianism. Alas! To slaughter their very bodies...
To devour its flesh—what could be more wicked, more poisonous, or more evil than such a heart? Where, then, can a good heart be found?
Now, when a creature sees a person wielding a blade, it never fails to tremble with fear and wail in grief; yet it is helpless, for its wisdom and strength cannot prevail against [the hunter].
Consequently, one will be killed by others. As recorded in the laws of cause and effect, to harbor grievance and seek retribution for one’s life is an inevitable principle of reality.
A poem says: "My flesh and the flesh of sentient beings differ in name but not in substance. Originally they share the same nature; it is only their physical forms that are distinct.

You undergo suffering and distress for their sake, while I consume their rich and sweet flavors for my own needs. Do not wait for Old Yan to pass judgment; examine this for yourself—what do you think? Now, as for killing...
Fortune was on the rise, yet military rebels filled the land; wherever one moved, there was slaughter. I have often seen those fleeing the chaos frequently encounter calamity by mere chance.
As the Buddha said: "When causes and conditions converge, retribution is difficult to escape. Those who commit acts of killing will inevitably suffer the retribution of being killed."
This is what is meant by that. Those who wish to turn the wheel of the kalpa should release living beings and refrain from killing;

those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land must recognize that food, sex, and their mutual causes—namely eating and drinking, and male and female—are the great desires of humanity. To restrain them as if they did not exist is the mark of a sage; one must not indulge in them.
To be wise is to exercise restraint; to indulge without moderation is to be foolish. These two states mutually assist one another in the creation of karma.
For when food and drink are abundant, the blood and vital energy flourish, which causes lustful desires to increase. When lustful desires increase, they in turn deplete the blood and vital energy.
Furthermore, one relies on food and drink for nourishment; if both can be reduced and frugally managed, this is the way to settle the body and prolong life.
Master Cijue said: "For humans, food and drink last as long as the sun and moon; whether fine or coarse, take what you need to fill the hungry gut.
