Once it has passed the three-inch gullet, what thing does it become? There is no need to use the mind to calculate it minutely. Wushi Yefu said: "Skin wrapping bone."
Flesh, pus, and blood—these are forcibly fashioned into seductive charms to delude people. It is because of this that heroes of a thousand ages have all fallen;
for a hundred years, we shall together become dust in a single pit. If one can truly observe the precepts regarding these two matters, how could there be illness or premature death in this world?
How could there be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals after death? If you wish to seek birth in the Pure Land, you must carefully guard yourself against these [distractions].
Constantly maintain your composure as if facing worldly objects such as wealth, beauty, fame, and profit. To illustrate this with a metaphor: suppose there were a mass of fire here. Five...
There are objects nearby. The first is like dry grass that ignites as soon as it is touched. The second is like wood that burns when blown upon.
The third is like iron, which cannot be made to burn; yet it can still be melted.
The fourth is like water, which not only does not burn but can actually extinguish fire; yet if it is contained within a cauldron or jar, it can still boil.

It is thus. Once its five [aggregates] are like space, one then allows them to be consumed by fire; the body remains eternally as it is and need not be extinguished, for it will extinguish itself naturally.
One begins by practicing and studying among ordinary beings, and only at the very end is one named a Great Sage, a Tathāgata.
If even a single thread of attachment to any worldly skills or miscellaneous arts, or indeed to anything— whether good or evil— that can divide one's mindfulness is not eliminated,
samādhi will not be achieved, and there will be no way to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Yet, all sentient beings today [are possessed of such attachments]...

The karmic consciousness is clearly pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; yet, should one give rise to even a single thought of worldly mind, one is immediately dragged away by such hosts of demons of defilement, causing the entire body to sink and perish, with no prospect of escape. It is like a wandering fish that, though free, [is caught].
Even a single thread that can be tied [to one’s heart] causes immense harm.

If you wish to sever the roots and stumps, and if you wish to bring an end to birth and death, you must cut off the very roots and stumps of birth and death. As the ancients said: "If craving is not severed, one will not be born in the Pure Land."
Thus we know that craving is the very root and trunk of birth and death. Tracing back this root of craving, it is not something possessed only in this present life.
Since beginningless time, through birth after birth and life after life, when has there ever been a single thought-moment free from this root of craving?

Now, as we practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, we must, in every thought-moment, sever this root of craving. Yet, in our daily lives, it manifests before us in the form of children, grandchildren, family affairs, and wealth.
In this world, there is not a single thing that is not love. It is as if one’s entire body were sitting in a pit of fire;

love is the sovereign, while mindfulness is merely the surface skin. For instance, when the sentiments of children and kin manifest before you, if you turn the light back upon yourself and examine them, can a single utterance of the Buddha-fruit oppose this love?
Can it sever this love? If you cannot oppose or sever it, how can you ever attain liberation?
Regarding birth and death: one must take up the single phrase "Buddha" and, in every thought-moment, strive to sever the very roots of this cycle of birth and death; only then will it be achieved.

For those who constantly recite the Buddha's name out of a desire to be reborn in a Pure Land, if they harbor even a slight attachment to this Sahā world in their ordinary moments, then when the time comes—
In the end, one will be pulled by this attachment and fail to be reborn there; how much more so when attachment is manifold?
Likewise, if there is even a single moment of mental discord at the time of death, one will be turned by that thought and fail to be reborn; how much more so when such thoughts are many?
Indeed, the nature of attachment varies in its degree—whether it be light or heavy, thick or thin. [This applies to] parents, wives, children, brothers, and...
Brothers, friends, fame and achievement, wealth and nobility, essays and poetic compositions,
arts and crafts, clothing and food, houses and fields, forests, springs, flowers, and fruits, precious jewels and playthings— these various wonders are beyond counting.
Whether great as Mount Tai or small as a goose’s down, if even one such thing remains cherished within the heart, then one will harbor [attachment].
Not a single thought. If thoughts are not unified, one cannot be born [there]. An ancient said: "If attachment is not profound, one will not be born in Saṃsāra;

if mindfulness is not unified, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. These two phrases may truly be called a golden scalpel for scraping away cataracts from the eyes, and a sacred medicine for curing chronic ailments.
All who are resolved to attain Sukhāvatī should inscribe this upon the walls of their dwellings and engrave it upon their hearts.
At all times, recite with solemnity; at every thought, maintain mindfulness. Regarding attachment to this Sahā world, strive daily to make it ever lighter;

regarding the thought of Sukhāvatī, strive daily to make it ever more singular. Make it lighter and yet lighter, gradually ascending until there is not even one [thought], and then again, there is the One.
One gradually approaches the ultimate fruit. If one can act in this way, then although one has not yet escaped Saṃsāra, one is no longer a long-term guest of Saṃsāra;
and although one has not yet been born in Sukhāvatī, one is already a distinguished guest of Sukhāvatī.

Supramundane filial piety consists of nourishing one’s parents with delicious food and drink, honoring them through noble rank and emolument, and manifesting their glory by cultivating virtue; this is mundane filial piety.

To exhort one’s parents to observe the precepts and uphold the Way, to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land, and to behold Amitābha face to face—this is supramundane filial piety.
To attain non-retrogression is the filial piety that transcends the world. For a child to repay their parents, this is what is most essential.

While the parents are alive and residing in the hall, one should encourage them early on to recite the Buddha’s name. After the parents have passed away, one should perform daily recitations for three years, or for one year, or for forty-nine days;
any of these durations is acceptable. A filial son who wishes to repay the debt of their parents' arduous toil must not fail to know this.

A child who assists their parents in traveling toward the West should attend to the service of filial piety. Observing that the time for their rebirth has arrived, they should compile a record of all the various good deeds performed by their parents throughout their lives and read it from time to time, causing their parents to feel great joy.
Furthermore, they should request their parents to sit or lie facing west and recite [the name of the Buddha].
Recite the name of Amitābha and set up an image to welcome them, as if they were already facing the Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the moment of passing away, one must further apply oneself with care;

do not allow the confusion of lamentation to disturb their right resolve. Recite the Buddha’s name together in unison to assist them in traveling to the West, so that they may personally attain birth in the Pure Land and enjoy all manner of bliss—is this not excellent?
True filial piety and support throughout one's life lie precisely in this moment.

Since you have already cultivated the Pure Land out of gratitude, you should now reflect upon that very gratitude. Setting aside for a moment the kindness of the Buddha and the kindness of the state, consider this:
is not the grace of one’s parents in raising and nurturing one not a profound kindness? Is not the virtue of one’s teachers in molding and perfecting one not a profound virtue? You must...
When you first left the home life, you spoke of repaying the heavy debt of gratitude; later, when traveling on pilgrimage, you again spoke of repaying the weight of profound virtue.
Having left your hometown and parted from your well for twenty or thirty years, you took no account at all of the hardships and sufferings endured by your parents and teachers.
When your parents grew old and sick, you did not care for them; even upon hearing of their deaths, you did not return. Now, perhaps you are among those in the third [state]...
On the road, you will undergo punishment and suffering, hoping that others will save you and hoping that others will deliver you.
Yet, if your mindfulness is interrupted at every thought-moment, the Pure Land will not be realized and you will be unable to save yourself. How then can you save others?

Since you cannot save one another, you are ungrateful and disloyal, a person of great filial impiety. As the Sutra says: "The sin of unfiliality shall cause one to fall into hell. Thus, even for a single thought-moment...
A distracted mind is itself the karma of hell. Furthermore, you do not weave yet have clothing; you do not plow yet have food;

your rooms, bedding, and requisites are provided for your use as if they were already there. You ought to diligently cultivate pure karma to repay the kindness of those who offer their faith and alms.

As the Patriarch said: "This is the portion of the donor and his wife; it is brought forth by their reduction and sacrifice. If your eye of the Way is not yet clear, even a drop of water [is not spared]."
Even for a single thread of silk, one must pull the plow and drag the harrow to repay the debt; only then can it be resolved.

If there is even a moment’s interruption in thought after thought, the Pure Land will not be realized. There is indeed a portion of this repayment to be made; thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of an animal.
Universally deliver all those who have received the instruction and admonition of teachers and friends, the guidance and support of benefactors, and the courtesy and hospitality of associates;

inform them all that they should repay these kindnesses by dedicating their merit to the Pure Land. This extends even to all people with whom one has shared so much as a single meal or a single cup of tea.

"O, how kind! Whether it be a single word or a brief meeting while seated, even down to those who serve as my slaves and labor for me, or anyone who exerts themselves in all matters concerning my daily needs—I address them all with this [teaching], desiring that they be liberated from the ocean of suffering.
It is not only these people; regarding everyone, whether known or unknown, recognized or unrecognized, I wish to transform them all through this, so that we may together..."
They shall be born in the Pure Land. It is not limited to these alone;

even down to all birds and beasts, as well as the crawling and wriggling species—indeed, all that has form and can be seen—whenever I behold them, I shall cause them to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha several times and make this vow:
"May you all be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss. After I have attained the Way, may [I lead] you all..."
"I shall deliver you all—not merely those who possess form, but even those who have reached the state where no marks can be perceived.

Thinking thus and making such a vow, my wholesome thoughts will become fully matured; then all sentient beings will become those with whom I share a karmic affinity, and when I transform and deliver them at a later time, there will be none among them who does not joyfully comply.

They mutually assist one another in performing all manner of good deeds: making offerings to the Buddhas and providing for the Sangha; constructing stupas and building monasteries; reciting mantras and performing repentance rituals; filially supporting their parents; being fraternal toward elder brothers and respectful toward younger brothers;
ensuring harmony among their clans and relatives; exchanging kindness and courtesy with those in their villages and neighborhoods; and serving their sovereign with loyalty.

The mind is the state. As an official, one is benevolent and compassionate, benefiting the people. As a leader, one is skillful in bringing peace to the multitude. As a subordinate, one is diligent in serving one's superiors.
One may instruct the ignorant and deluded; assist the orphaned and the weak; rescue those in urgent distress; bestow gifts upon the poor;
construct bridges and pave wells; distribute food and dispense medicine; or reduce one’s own provisions for the sake of others.
Benefiting others: whether by being generous with wealth and reflecting upon oneself, or by teaching others to do good, or by protecting virtue and restraining evil—
whatever worldly or world-transcending wholesome deeds one performs, regardless of their magnitude—

even if it be merely giving a single coin to another or quenching someone’s thirst with a single drink, down to even the slightest virtue of a hair’s breadth— one must invariably give rise to this thought:
May these virtuous conditions be dedicated toward the Western Land. May all wholesome deeds support one another so that rebirth there may certainly be attained.
Practice without blemish and accomplish the eight dharmas; by practicing without blemish in this world, one will be born in the Pure Land. What are these eight?

They benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward in return. Whatever merits they perform when all sentient beings undergo various sufferings and afflictions, they bestow them all entirely upon those beings.
They regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind, remaining humble and without obstruction. Toward all bodhisattvas, they look as they would upon a Buddha.
When hearing sutras they have not heard before, they do not harbor doubts. They do not conflict with the śrāvakas, nor are they envious of others.

He makes offerings without exalting his own benefit, but within that practice he disciplines his mind; he constantly examines his own faults and does not speak of the shortcomings of others, always seeking all manner of merit with a single-minded focus.
If sentient beings give rise to ten kinds of mind and single-mindedly direct them toward the Buddha, such persons shall attain rebirth at the end of their lives.
First, they give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and harbor no intent to harm. Second, toward all sentient beings...
1. To give rise to great compassion and a mind free from affliction; 2. To cherish one’s body and life for the sake of the Buddha’s true Dharma, with a mind that delights in its protection;
3. To generate supreme patience toward all phenomena, with a mind free from attachment; 4.
To have no craving for gain, offerings, honor, or respect, with a mind of pure intention; 5. To seek the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes at all times.
1. A mind free from forgetfulness. 2. Toward all sentient beings, one holds them in esteem and respect, without a sense of inferiority. 3.
One does not cling to worldly discourse, but gives rise to a mind of certainty regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
4. One plants various roots of goodness with a mind that is untainted and pure. 5. Toward all Tathāgatas, one abandons all signs (*nimitta*) and gives rise to a mind of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
If one attains even one of these ten states of mind, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
Regarding the fourfold analysis of having Chan but no Pure Land: "Nine out of ten go astray; when the realm of the *ālaya* manifests, they are instantly carried away by it."
If there is no Chan but there is Pure Land, ten thousand who practice will all go [to rebirth]. Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
If there is both Chan and Pure Land, one is like a tiger with horns; in this life one becomes a teacher of men, and in the future one becomes a Buddha or Patriarch.
Without dhyāna there is no Pure Land; there are only the iron bed and the copper pillar. Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one has no one to rely upon.

Just as day must be prepared for by night, and one must prepare for the night; as heat must be prepared for by cold, and one must prepare for the cold; so too, existence must be prepared for by departure.

One must certainly prepare for departure. What constitutes preparation for the night? Lamps, candles, bedding, and mats. What constitutes preparation for the cold? Quilts, furs, charcoal, and firewood.
What constitutes preparation for departure? Merit, wisdom, and the Pure Land.

One should study this Dharma, which is the direct path for the peaceful cultivation and purification of karma, easy to practice. All Mahāyāna sūtras proclaim this essential point, and there are none among the Buddhas of the ten directions who do not praise it.
Whether they be bhikṣus, the fourfold assembly, or virtuous sons and daughters of faith, those who wish to swiftly shatter ignorance and [attain] eternal...
One who wishes to extinguish the grave offenses of the five heinous acts and the ten evil deeds, as well as other minor transgressions, should practice this Dharma.
One who desires to attain purity, and to be fully endowed with all the gates of the *pāramitās* according to the major and minor codes of discipline, should study this Dharma.

One who desires to be free from all fears at the time of death, to have peace and happiness in body and mind, to feel joy like returning home, and to have one’s dwelling illuminated by light and filled with extraordinary fragrances and sounds, should study this Dharma.
Joy! Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of sages, shall send forth a purple-golden platform and extend his hand to welcome you.

Crossing the five paths and traversing the nine grades, you shall cast off the torments of heat and find rest in cool serenity. Having just left behind worldly toil, you shall immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression;

without passing through long kalpas, you shall realize the state of non-arising. Those who wish to practice even a small portion of the Dharma and thereby receive such a response should study this method. If you desire to cultivate even a minor dharma, yet seek to be moved by its grace...
This is a wondrous reward. The Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously offer praise and bestow a prophecy in their presence. In a single thought-moment, one makes offerings to countless Buddhas;
returning to one's own land, one sits and eats together with Amitābha, engages in discourse with Avalokiteśvara, and follows the steps of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

One possesses clear vision and penetrating hearing, with a physical form of boundless dimensions. Moving freely through the air, one clearly understands past lives and surveys the five realms of existence as if they were before one’s eyes. As it is said:
Like a reflection in a mirror, one enters the inexhaustible samādhi moment by moment; one should practice this sublime dharma.

Regarding rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha via the "three-pronged cord," there are three powers: first, the power of the inherently existing Buddha-nature, which refers to [the Buddha-nature] within the mind of afflictions.

First, there is the Tathāgatagarbha. Second, the power of compassionate light that gathers and protects: it is said that Amitābha’s light is immeasurable, and he gathers and never abandons those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Third, the power of the *nien-fo* samādhi: it is said that by recollecting and mindfully contemplating the Buddha, [one attains this state].
"In the present and in the future, you will certainly behold the Buddha. These three powers are like three strands of rope joined together to form a great cord, capable of pulling heavy objects.
Furthermore, they are like water, fire, and a mirror: if one holds them toward the sun and uses moxa to collect it, one can obtain fire;
if one holds them toward the moon and uses a gem to collect it, one can obtain water. Now, the mirror possesses water.
The nature of fire is a metaphor for the fundamental power of the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings.

That it requires the light of the sun and moon to shine upon it refers to the power of Amitābha’s compassionate light to gather and embrace them. That the pearl and the tinder can draw forth water and fire refers to the power of faith and the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
When these three factors harmonize, water and fire are produced; when these three powers mutually support one another, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
Although beginningless evil karma may be heavy when weighed, ten recitations at the moment of death can counteract it. Now, this shall be compared by way of three aspects.
First, when one creates evil in the mind, it arises from false and inverted views; whereas the practitioner of Buddha-remembrance hears [the teachings] from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
The names and titles of the Buddha’s true merits consist of one reality and one unreality; how could they possibly be compared? It is like a dark room ten thousand years old:
when the sunlight briefly reaches it, how could the long-accumulated darkness fail to be extinguished?

Second, at the time of committing offenses through conditions, arising from a mind of deluded darkness and conditioned by false objects, one gives rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha through hearing.

Regarding the names and titles of the Buddha’s merits, when conditioned by the unsurpassed bodhicitta, one may arise as either truly genuine or falsely counterfeit; how could these possibly be compared?
It is like a person struck by a poisoned arrow, where the shaft is deep and the venom is cruel, wounding the flesh and breaking the bone.

Upon hearing the drum of the medicine that eradicates it, the arrow immediately emerges and the poison is removed. How could it be that because the arrow is deep and the poison is cruel, the arrow would not be extracted? Thirdly...

At the moment one definitely commits a transgression, there is an interval and a subsequent thought; however, at the moment one recollects the Buddha, there is no interval and no subsequent thought, and one immediately passes away.
Because the wholesome mind is so intense and sharp, one is reborn [in that state] immediately. It is like a great rope ten spans in circumference.

A thousand men could not restrain him; yet a youth brandished his sword and in an instant split [the mountain] in two. It was like a thousand-year-old pile of firewood that is consumed in a short time by a single grain of fire.
To leave the household life merely by shaving one's hair and donning dyed robes is what people call "leaving home. Alas, this is nothing more than leaving behind the gates of one’s own family;
it is not truly leaving the burning house of the triple world. Whenever I see someone newly ordained, there is none who does not possess a certain degree of... [text fragment ends]

At first he was well-intentioned, but after some time, he became entangled by causes and conditions. Tainted by fame and profit, he subsequently began to adorn his clothing, acquire land and property, maintain a retinue of disciples, and accumulate vast quantities of gold and silk. He busied himself with worldly affairs until he was no different from a layperson.
As the sutras state, "When one person leaves the household life, Pāpīyān trembles with fear. Now that this man has become like this, Pāpīyān may surely pour out wine to celebrate!

When one’s head is rubbed, one thinks of cold; when hungry, one thinks of food; when dwelling, one thinks of security; when using utensils, one thinks of sufficiency; having a son, one thinks of his marriage; having a daughter, one thinks of her dowry;
in studying, one thinks of obtaining rank and emolument; in managing a household, one thinks of becoming wealthy and prosperous. Yet, at times, these things are not obtained.

"Let it go. It is for the sake of being free from such burdens that one resolutely leaves the household life. Yet, if one still remains mindful of various worldly concerns, what is the value of leaving the household life?
The Buddha said: "Constantly rub your own head to cast off ornaments and finery. But this applies not only to ornaments;
one should constantly rub one's own head, saying, "I am a monk," and suddenly abandon all external conditions to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

The King of Physicians regards all teachers as World-Honored Ones. If there is one who can explain profound meanings and unravel the knots of doubt, thereby benefiting him, he will honor them with his whole heart and mind, never dwelling on their faults.
It is like a worn-out sack containing precious jewels; one does not [discard the sack because of its condition].
Because the person is evil, one does not take the treasure. It is also like traveling at night on a dangerous path where an evil person holds up a torch;
one does not refuse the light because of the person's wickedness. As the Sūtra says: "One should conceive the thought of sickness and suffering regarding one's own body;

the thought of a king of physicians regarding the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); the thought of excellent medicine regarding the Dharma taught; and the thought of curing the disease regarding the practice undertaken."
If one hears a single phrase of a previously unheard Dharma, it is superior to obtaining the three-thousandfold world system filled with the seven treasures,
as well as the positions of Śakra, Brahmā, and a Cakravartin King. [The six sense faculties...]
A thousand varieties of adornment are for the sake of the half-inch eye; a hundred kinds of music are for the sake of the bean-sized ear;
aloeswood, sandalwood, brain-scented musk, and musk deer are for the sake of the two apertures of the nose; food spread over ten feet square is for the sake of the three-inch tongue.
Exquisite beauty and seductive charm exist solely for the sake of this foul and decaying body; compliance and flattery exist solely for the sake of a wild and dissolute mind.

If one can discern this principle and is no longer deluded by the six sense organs, then there will be no afflictions. Although one has not yet been born in the Pure Land, one is already as if born there.

If, when encountering objects, one’s mind harbors doubt for even a single thought-moment, one is obstructed by earth; if one’s mind harbors attachment for a single thought-moment, one is drowned by water;

if one’s mind harbors anger for a single thought-moment, one is burned by fire; if one’s mind harbors joy for a single thought-moment, one is blown away by wind. If you can discern this in such a way, you will not be so overcome.
The objects of perception transform. In every place, one employs these objects. The way to employ these objects must begin with the single mind of right mindfulness.
Setting aside the mark of self, contemplate truthfully: before this body was born, did it have form? Did it have a name? Did it have a self? Once the body has dissolved...
What are these appearances? What is this so-called "name"? What is this "self"? Before the body and after the body, both are unknowable.

How can one, in the midst of this, perversely cling to it as a self, becoming attached, anxious, and fearful, remaining sorrowful all day long? To escape such sorrow, nothing is better than reciting the Buddha’s name.
The mind is empty and its principle is tranquil;

yet ordinary people are mostly obstructed by phenomena regarding principle and obstructed by objects regarding the mind. They constantly seek to flee from objects in order to settle the mind and dismiss phenomena, remaining unaware that they are actually obstructing objects with the mind and obstructing principle with phenomena.
One need only allow the mind to be empty and the objects will naturally become empty; so too with principle.
The quiescence of phenomena is itself quiescent.
When the mind ceases, the nature of stillness manifests as its essence; the mind resides therein. Movement constitutes the mind; the nature resides therein. Thus, the mind arises.
The nature of phenomena ceases; when the mind ceases, the true nature manifests, like the moon appearing when clouds disperse, or the mirror becoming bright when dust is cleared away.

The nature of karma is empty, yet ordinary beings merely perceive the power of karma as dense and habitual; they do not know that the nature of karma is fundamentally empty. If sentient beings’ karma...

Regarding the reality of nature: throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, there is no place for it to be contained. It is like black clouds obstructing the sky; when the wind arrives, they are extinguished.

If the clouds were real, they would not disperse even if blown by the wind. Empty space is a metaphor for nature; the black clouds are a metaphor for karma; and mindfulness of the Buddha is a metaphor for the wind.
Therefore, through delusion one enters the prison of the womb; through mindfulness one enters the lotus calyx.

Just as a dung-worm in its latrine cannot be pulled out even by ten thousand oxen—though a dog or a sheep looking upon it would find it unbearable in its suffering—the dung-worm itself does not realize this.
Suffering is what they take for pleasure. When dogs and sheep are on the ground, from a human perspective their suffering is unbearable, yet the dogs and sheep do not know suffering;
they take it for pleasure. From the perspective of Heaven, so it is with humans in this world.

They cannot overcome their suffering, yet people do not realize they are suffering; instead, they regard it as pleasure. If one extends this logic to its ultimate conclusion, the pleasure and pain of heaven are likewise the same.
Knowing this, those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land cannot be turned back even by ten thousand oxen.

One maintains the human relations and the myriad things, each and every one unimpeded by the Way. What is valued is simply to act according to principle and respond to conditions, following along with them without a deliberate mind.
As the Sutra says: "Internally cultivating the practices of a Bodhisattva, externally manifesting the body of a Śrāvaka. Today, one harbors within the transcendental world.
It is permissible for the mind to manifest worldly phenomena externally. In this way, the family and household will find peace of mind.

Having attained mastery over entering and exiting [the world], liberation does not consist in the deliberate application of mental effort; rather, it is precisely through the absence of such effort that one is liberated. Simply maintain single-minded right mindfulness;
there is no need to urgently seek spiritual efficacy. It is like traveling on a road: by walking without ceasing, one will naturally arrive at home. As for the timing, it depends only on...
In this state, maintain a single thought with endurance and without interruption; do not allow a desire for haste to take hold of it.
One should view wealth and honor solely from the perspective of one's own poverty and low station; seeing their blazing aura of power, one must not succumb to the longing of drooling envy. However...

Those who encounter such things do not necessarily experience true happiness, nor are these matters of vital importance. For instance, food serves to stave off hunger and clothing to ward off the cold;
yet if one’s clothing is ornate or one’s food is exquisite, what essential benefit does this bring to the body and mind? Other matters may be understood by extension from this principle.
As for the ultimate points of great profit or harm—old age, sickness, and death—one must face them alone with this single body.
It is like casting one’s final die when the bell has tolled and the water-clock has run out; from emperors and ministers down to the common people, there is no one who can take one’s place.
All must reach their end together, without the addition of even a hair’s breadth. When one reflects upon this, who could fail to feel immediate trepidation?
One should only focus the mind on right mindfulness to seek the sovereign wealth and honor of Sukhāvatī.
The carefree and joyful widowers, widows, orphans, and solitary individuals—viewed through the eyes of the mundane world, these are the most pitiable;

yet among all those in the world, none are more carefree or joyful than these four kinds of people. It is a pity that they do not know to take refuge in the Pure Land. Otherwise, [they would attain liberation].
Since there is nothing to rely upon before one's eyes, after death one will inevitably fall into the cycle of saṃsāra.

People today merely fail to realize this because they regard their households as too important and their kin as too real. Even those of noble character and wisdom may be able to treat fame and office lightly and remain content in poverty and low station;

yet when it comes to their children, they absolutely cannot bring themselves to cast them off, instead willingly becoming like oxen and horses for their sake. Before the child has even reached maturity...
The woman comes again, and the man is fortunate enough to marry her; yet the woman urges him to wed once more.
Thus it goes, from turmoil to further turmoil—where could one find the leisure for reciting the Buddha’s name? Having no desire at all to endure such things, what concern is this of yours?
It would be better to be as pure as the four types of people mentioned; one should instead live with carefree ease, taking advantage of this very opportunity. Now is the right time.
It is well to focus one's mind on practice and leap out of birth and death; such a person is truly the most joyful in all the world.
Generally speaking, in human life, the less attachment there is, the fewer the bonds; the fewer the bonds, the fewer the karmic obstructions.
One’s ties to worldly conditions will be shallow, while one’s affinity with the Buddha will be deep. Quickly and diligently recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the preservation of life while forgetting death, people of the world merely know how to nourish and care for this body during their lifetime, seeking out the means to support it; yet they do not contemplate relinquishing this body.
Afterward, the consciousness does not perish. If one lacks virtuous causes, one will fall into the miserable realms. Why then, during one's lifetime, do you cherish [the body] so?

"Do you not contemplate the liberation of this body after death? Furthermore, worldly people devote themselves exclusively to their wives, children, and kin, laboring extensively to provide food and clothing without the slightest negligence, yet they do not consider the time of their own demise.

At that time, though one's wife, children, and kin may love one to the marrow of one's bones, they cannot rescue one; one must go forth alone. I now exhort worldly people: for the sake of sustaining life, one ought not—"
One forgets the fear of death. One should not, for the sake of other matters, forget to act for one's own benefit.
These five delusions cause people of this land not to be weary of the clamor and bustle of the secular world, yet to long for the tranquility of an araṇya (forest hermitage). Therefore, there are...

To praise with such earnestness the act of leaving home and becoming a monk, yet not wish to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—despite the fact that the myriad sufferings of this Sahā world are far more than mere clamor, while the leisurely ease of Sukhāvatī is vastly superior even to an araṇya—is the first delusion. They recognize the beauty of renunciation, yet do not aspire for rebirth there. This is their first confusion.
Those who have traveled ten thousand li with arduous toil to seek out a spiritual teacher do so for the purpose of illuminating the Great Matter and resolving the questions of birth and death.

As for the World-Honored One Amitābha, his physical and mental karma are supreme and his power of vows is vast and profound; when he utters a single perfect sound, there is nothing it does not clearly harmonize with.

To wish to associate with those of learning yet not desire to see the Buddha—this is the second delusion. To delight in dwelling within vast monastic communities yet not wish to rely upon small-scale centers for the Way;

and while the number of those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss who are in their final birth before Buddhahood is exceedingly great, where all supreme virtuous people gather in one place, to desire to draw near to monastic communities yet not admire that purity.
O Assembly of the Pure Ocean: their delusions are threefold. The people of this region do not exceed a hundred years in maximum lifespan;

yet they are beset by childhood ignorance, senility, and chronic illness. Torpor and sleep occupy more than half of their time. Even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "darkness between the aggregates" (*antarābhava*).

If even the Śrāvakas are still dimly aware of emerging from the womb, then of every inch of jade and every minute of time, nine-tenths are lost before they have attained the stage of non-retrogression;
this is truly cause for heartache. The people of the Western [Land] possess immeasurable lifespans; once entrusted to the lotus-womb, they never again suffer the pain of death.

One then attains the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) and the certainty of the Buddha-stage. While the duration of existence in the *Saha* world is brief, one fails to realize that the Pure Land offers eternal life;

this is the fourth delusion. Only when one’s rank is fixed in non-retrogression and the fruit of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the realization of the non-arising of phenomena) is realized—such that one is free from desire while amidst desire and remains undefiled while dwelling in the dust of the world—can one then exercise compassion rooted in the same essence as all beings and harmonize with the light within the five turbidities. As for those who...
With meager learning and superficial wisdom, they immediately claim to transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*), yet they remain attached to this Sahā world and disparage the Pure Land.
Thus they wander aimlessly, following one after another into the hells. Who could compare such people to these Great Power Bodhisattvas? This is their fifth delusion.

Those who study the Buddha-dharma in this world willingly submit themselves to suffering and hardship; yet at the outset, there is none among them who does not say, "The matter of birth and death is great.

However, once moved by fame and profit or muddied by worldly entanglements, they set aside this great matter of birth and death without further discussion. Or, when questioned or challenged by others...
Thus, others offer excuses and evasions, unable to reach a definitive conclusion. Some say, "There is no need to ask this. Others say, "It is unnecessary to know.
Still others say, "When the official tally arrives, simply carry it out; do not engage in deliberation. Some say, "One will take birth wherever one may, with freedom of movement.
Others say, "For now, you shall be born into a family that is neither high nor low, and again obtain a male body. Yet others say, "Grasp firmly the vital essence (*bindu*)."

The gods perceive the signs of good and evil, yet they cannot follow [the deceased] away. Some cause them to wait in anticipation to know the time; some instruct them to seize the *ālaya-vijñāna* (the store-consciousness) at the moment of death;

some say that while the hundred skeletal parts disintegrate, one thing remains eternally spiritual; others say that when the form disperses and the breath vanishes, all returns to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Such various conjectures and deceptions do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
When the four great elements dissolve and one is oppressed by the suffering of illness, the consciousness has no master and follows karma in saṃsāra—of this there is no doubt.
Even if one were to fix a date and set a time to sit and depart or stand and transform, such worldly virtues may be achieved, yet they are not sufficient to be considered extraordinary.
This arises from not having seen the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations), not knowing the characteristics of rebirth in the nine grades, and lacking faith in the power of Amitābha’s vows,
while stubbornly clinging to one's own views and willingly enduring suffering like being smeared with pitch and scorched in fire— is this not truly pitiable?

To contemplate the Buddha with a mind of false views is to rely on external objects to manifest one's nature. When each thought is free from dependence and every phenomenon is entirely true, those who do not understand will recklessly give rise to doubt and slander.
Thus, there are those who cling to the idea that the internal mind is the Buddha and refuse to seek it externally, clinging to their own [limited perspective].
Those who claim there is no Buddha and thus do not require another Buddha; those who cling to the emptiness of all phenomena and do not believe in the existence of a Buddha;

those who cling to the idea that everything is spontaneously accomplished and does not depend upon cultivation or realization—these individuals merely fail to follow the holy teachings and fail to penetrate the essence of reality.
Whatever one clings to becomes a false view; one denies cause and effect, indulges in deluded sentiments, mistakes gravel for gold, and attempts to cook rice by steaming sand.

Some arrogant ones say: "If one sees one's nature and awakens to the Way, one immediately transcends birth and death; what need is there to fixate the mind on that Buddha or seek rebirth in another land?
However, a true practitioner should examine themselves. As the saying goes, "When a person drinks water, they know its coldness or warmth for themselves. Thus, observe yourself.

In their practice and realization, they have seen their nature and awakened to the Way; they have received the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the position of the Patriarchs—can they compare to Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna?
Having attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, can they compare to the Tiantai Master Zhiyi?

They have mastered both the doctrine and its exposition, cultivating both practice and realization—can they compare to National Teacher Huizhong? All these great beings clearly elucidated the teachings of the scriptures.

I earnestly exhort you to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land]. This is for the benefit of both yourself and others; how could one be willing to mislead others and bring harm upon oneself? Furthermore, you should reflect for yourself:
at the time of death, will you truly attain mastery over whether you depart or remain? Since beginningless time, your heavy karmic obstructions have been profound.
Will you certainly not manifest [in samsara] again until this retribution-body is exhausted? Will you certainly be liberated from the cycle of rebirth?

Within the three evil realms, will you certainly be free to appear and disappear at will, without suffering or affliction? Throughout the heavens, the human world, and the worlds of the ten directions, will you certainly have no hindrance in resting wherever you please?
If you can attain such clear self-confidence, what could be more excellent than this? If you have not yet reached it, do not— [The original text ends abruptly here.]
For a time, through arrogance, one instead brings about eternal sinking into saṃsāra; having lost one's own opportunity for spiritual benefit, whom else can one blame?

Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha today are called "exclusive practitioners. As for praying for longevity, there is the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*; as for the expiation of sins, [there is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*].
If you have transgressions, there is the *Lianghuang Chàn*; if you face calamities and hardships, there is the *Xiāozāi Zhòu*; if you seek wisdom, there is the *Guānyīn Wén*.

As for the Buddha you have been recollecting, you have relegated it to a high shelf; if this provides no benefit to your actual affairs, consider that the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable—how much more so, then, your own hundred-year lifespan?
Consider that that Buddha is able to extinguish the heavy burden of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
How much more so, then, for the defilements, calamities, and hardships present before one’s eyes! One does not reflect upon those words of that Buddha:

"I shall illuminate the boundless realms extensively with the light of wisdom. How much less, then, regarding the so-called "wisdom" of people in this age? It is like the *agada* medicine, which holds mastery over all myriad ailments.
Their minds are divided and wavering; none are willing to believe or submit. As for this divine sagacity and exquisite craftsmanship, what indeed can be done about it?

Regarding the prevention of death, people of the world have a saying: "Accumulate moments of joy to prevent death. The meaning of this is that human existence is too bitter and the fleeting life is too [short].
Hastening. How does this differ from rushing to offer thanks in a state of panic? It is like indulging in pleasure to enjoy rest.

Should one by chance pass away along with the transformations of nature, and reflect upon one's entire life, there will surely have been many joyful matters. Compared to those who spend their whole lives in poverty and distress, is this not a victory over them by a single stroke?
If it were truly so, it would be like adding weight to a shoulder-load or pouring more wood onto a boiling cauldron; this is called "hastened death. What is meant by this?

To prevent death is the foremost concern; nothing compares to resolving the matter of birth and death. To resolve the matter of birth and death, nothing compares to reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
Furthermore, there is a class of people who are shrouded by worldly tastes and cannot attain [liberation]. They take loftiness as their ambition and leisure as their disposition.
Some seek to refine their emotions through poetry and wine, or exchange the concerns of this world for a game of chess. Others settle their minds upon the Five Peaks.

Chanting and whistling amidst the mists and clouds—these are all those who vainly waste their time. Even the ten classes of flying immortals and the feathered guests of the Three Mountains are not without their own sense of carefree transcendence and pride in their spiritual ascension;
yet they can do nothing about the fact that their true nature remains unilluminated and the cycle of birth and death remains unresolved.
The Buddha has spoken of many precedents, stating that "human life lies between a single inhalation and exhalation. This phrase is not difficult to understand in its underlying meaning;
you have personally seen it with your eyes and heard it with your ears through many such precedents, just as occurred during the funeral rites of the other day.
When a monk passes away, one should be somber and unhappy, earnestly exhorting one another, saying:
"O Great Assembly, today we escort this monk, and tomorrow we shall escort that monk; before we know it, it will be our own turn. At that time, regret will be of no avail.
We must diligently and urgently recite the Buddha's name, never letting a single moment slip by. This is truly how one ought to speak whenever the opportunity arises.

To speak of it as something to be regretted is already too late; once the moment has passed, one continues to laugh and talk as usual. It is simply that people do not believe their lives are but a breath away—laughing and weeping.
When an infant is born, they weep before they even smile; is this not the great suffering of existence? Since birth, as soon as I have emerged into the world, I have entered the realm of weeping.
Thereafter, instances of smiling are few while instances of weeping are many; moments of laughter are short while periods of crying are long.
Until the bell tolls and the water-clock runs out, one ultimately disperses after a great bout of weeping. It is either I who am weeping for others, or others who are weeping for me.
People come and go, weeping for one another. If you wish to avoid such weeping, you must make a vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
how could there ever be any cause for weeping then?
Virtue is difficult to produce in the young;
in this world, the mind for doing good is slight, while the mind for doing evil is heavy. When facing a Buddha image, one is not as reverent as when receiving a great guest;
in studying the sutras and the Dharma, one is not as diligent as when seeking wealth and profit; and in slandering others, one’s breath is coarse and one’s words are harsh.
If one praises another with a slippery tongue, their breath will become sluggish and their speech stilted. If one dislikes someone, they will conceal that person's virtues and broadcast their faults;
if one likes someone, they will hide their shortcomings and magnify their strengths. Some accumulate evil and harbor anger toward others through private slanders;

some perform minor acts of goodness yet resent those around them. Regarding evil deeds, they may secretly squander a thousand pieces of gold; yet regarding good people, they are able to restrain their tongues and practice generosity. Only then is one a true person of virtue.
To prepare a single meal and then boast of one's own merit, hoping to be reborn in the Pure Land on account of such a minor good deed—this is difficult.

To use wax seals to stamp upon clay, thereby slandering the Buddha and defaming the sutras, constitutes the five heinous crimes and the four grave offenses; all are accomplished by a single thought of evil karma, leading to a fall into the Avīci Hell, just as...

When an arrow is shot, it reaches its mark; likewise, the present recollection of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land are accomplished by a single thought of wholesome karma, and one immediately ascends to Sukhāvatī as easily as bending an arm.

The preceding thought-moment of the five aggregates ceases, and the succeeding thought-moment of the five aggregates arises—just as when a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal is destroyed while the impression is formed.
This does not even require two thought-moments. For instance, when the novice monk Kṣīrapriya gave rise to a single thought of craving for curd, he was subsequently reborn as curd.
Worms form within it; all these are produced by a single thought-moment.
As for a hundred catties of gold—if a person possesses a hundred catties of gold and suddenly encounters a great calamity, they cannot carry it away on their back; they must inevitably abandon it.
Suppose one were to carry gold with them and die together with it; the world would surely call such a person "greatly foolish.

This is because they know that this body is more precious than a hundred *jin* of gold. Yet, in their daily lives, they frantically pursue fame and compete for profit, refusing to relinquish even an object worth a hundred coins, while failing to cherish their own bodies. Why is it that they do not seek birth in the Pure Land?

An ancient verse concerning the verification of rebirth states: "The sages are born from the crown; those born in the heavens from the eyes; humans from the heart; hungry ghosts from the belly; animals from within the knees;

and those in hell emerge from the soles of the feet. When such a person dies, one examines their residual warmth to know the place of their rebirth. This is because the mind dwelt in meditative stillness (*dhyāna*).
Thus, that which is light and pure condenses within; when the emotions are obstructed by love and hatred, one becomes heavy and turbid, clinging to material things.
That which is light flies beyond the clouds and does not sink; that which is heavy sinks like a stone and cannot be lifted upward. Accumulated over a lifetime, this is self-evident at the end.

Regarding the two sufferings of birth and death, as for the suffering of birth: one takes up semen and blood as a physical body; dwelling between the stomach and the large intestine, it undergoes forty-two transformations to become this illusory substance.
Above, one is oppressed by foul food; below, one is suffocated by a stinking pit. Drinking cold, it is like an icy river; swallowing heat, it is like furnace coals. Thus it is.

They become dazed and bewildered, beyond all description. When the time of birth arrives, the various sufferings are immeasurable. As they touch the hand and fall to the ground, it is like being flayed alive;

as they are forced through the birth canal with great difficulty, it is like a tortoise struggling to emerge from its shell. Clutching their grievances and harboring resentment, they are dizzy and disoriented.

As soon as they encounter the warm wind, the conditions of their suffering are suddenly forgotten. They become infants, foolish and ignorant, yet may meet with untimely death by water or fire. Only after escaping these perils do they come into being.

Regarding humans: when the seeds for the cultivation of the body have ripened in the field of karma, they are frequently nourished by the waters of craving. Ignorance arises, and the sprouts of suffering grow.
Adhering like glue to the seven consciousnesses and enveloping the nine abodes, they revolve like a whirling firebrand, circling without end. This is the suffering of death.
The wind-sword dismembers the body; the fire-element burns the frame. Within, the voice trembles in emptiness; the *po* and *hun* spirits quiver with terror.

Utmost suffering arises all at once, and evil karma suddenly manifests. A thousand sorrows press down in melancholy, and ten thousand fears cause frantic alarm. Even until life expires and the breath ceases, one departs alone in silence.
The nether path is dark and gloomy; the road to the underworld is vast and boundless. There, one meets former enemies face-to-face in stark clarity, crying out to Heaven.
Striking the ground, they seek liberation but find no door. Following the shallowness or depth of their karma, they pass through the various realms of existence;

some are born head-downward in the hells, while others secretly assume the forms of hungry ghosts. They endure hunger and thirst, wailing for long kalpas, and suffer the pains of retribution until their entire bodies are scorched and rotting.

As long as one has not yet escaped the karmic retribution of good and evil within the twenty-five realms of existence, there is nothing that perishes; the body receives its retribution in pursuit, never being lost or omitted.

The ocean of birth and death is vast, and the paths of karma are difficult to exhaust. Even Śrāvakas remain obscured, and Bodhisattvas who have recently emerged from the womb are still dim-sighted while passing through the "shading of the corpse."
How much more so for ordinary beings bound by all fetters—how could they not be shackled by the Mara of birth and death?

Among the ten difficulties, the first is that one does not always encounter a Buddha. In the perilous paths of the triple world, the Buddha is the guide; yet the karma of sentient beings is heavy, and thus they are born at times when they do not encounter him.
First, because the Buddha Śākyamuni has already passed into extinction and Maitreya has not yet appeared, the noble sages are hidden and obscured, and false teachings flourish;
thus, one does not hear the preaching of the Dharma. Second, in this degenerate age of the Semblance Dharma, all speech consists only of the heterodox and evil discourses of outsiders;
because the True Dharma is not heard, one does not encounter it. Third, one is entangled by evil friends and associates who seek only gain and offerings, fanning delusion and leading one astray.
1. Because people fall into the evil realms; 2. Because the four classes of Māras harass and disturb them; 3.

Because the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist heretics and wicked people destroy and disrupt the True Dharma, preventing practitioners from achieving accomplishment; 4. Because the cycle of rebirth does not cease, as they revolve through the six destinies like a water-drawing wheel, without rest;
5. Because it is difficult to escape the evil realms, as they come and go within the three worlds, receiving retribution according to their karma.

1. Although one may be born in the heavens, one cannot avoid eventual decline and fall. 2. Seven types of worldly conditions obstruct the Path; being submerged in the toil of mundane existence constitutes an obstacle to transcending the world.
3. Life spans are short and fleeting; of those who live a hundred years, many meet with untimely death, and time passes so rapidly that it is difficult for a Bodhisattva to accomplish the Great Way.
4. There is regression and loss in spiritual practice; practicing in this land [of Jambudvīpa] involves interruptions.

Only when the afflictions of views and thought are eliminated can one avoid falling back; for practitioners at the initial stage cannot yet avoid retrogression. Thus, it is difficult to achieve success in ten *rajas-kalpas*.

This is like those who heard the Dharma during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū: having regressed from the Great Vehicle and clung to the Lesser, they remained on the level of the Śrāvaka for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Although this spanned a vast duration of time, they had not yet accomplished the Great Way.

Sentient beings, driven by their thoughts and desires, fly up or fall down throughout all worlds, their birth and death continuing in succession. Birth follows from habitual tendencies; death follows from the flow of transformation.

At the moment of passing away, before warmth and sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one's entire life manifest simultaneously. If one’s thoughts are purely positive, one will surely fly upward and be born in the heavens.

If, while flying in the mind, one possesses both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open; one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands, and will be reborn therein according to one's vows.
If one’s emotions are slight and thoughts are many, one will be lightly raised up, yet not far away, becoming an Immortal Who Flies.

When emotion (*kleśa*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among human beings. When thought is clear, one is intelligent; when emotion is profound, one is dull-witted.

When emotion is predominant and thought is slight, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth (*tiryagyoni*); the heavy become the fur-bearing herds, while the light become the feathered tribes. This occurs when there are seven emotions and three thoughts.
Sinking down into the water-wheel, they are born at the boundary of fire. Receiving the breath of fierce flames, their bodies become those of hungry ghosts who are constantly scorched.

Water can only harm them; without food or drink, they pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas. With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of the intellect, they descend into the wheel of fire.

Those who slight their lives fall into the *sāntara* hells; those who value their lives fall into the *avīci* hells. These two types of hell are for those of purely deluded nature who sink directly into the Avīci Hell.

If they sink into the intermediate states of mind, it is because they have slandered the Mahāyāna, violated the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, spoken deceptive and false teachings, or vainly craved offerings of faith.
They have unwarrantedly received honor and respect. Yet those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses will be reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions.
Good causes lead to evil fruits;

as it is today, there are those in the world who understand Chan and understand the Way, numbering like the sands of the Ganges River, and who speak of the Buddha and speak of the mind, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and myriads.

Even with a hundred million [eons], if not even a speck of dust [of defilement] is exhausted, one cannot escape saṃsāra; if not even a single thread-thin thought is forgotten, one will entirely fall into ruin.

Those of such a kind cannot even recognize themselves, yet they falsely speak of karmic retribution, claiming to benefit both self and others, and considering themselves superior to their predecessors.
They merely say that whatever meets the eye is nothing but the Buddha’s work, and every step taken is entirely a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Yet, if one examines what they actually practice:
It is not as good as being an ordinary person who observes the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. Observe their speech: they disparage the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Yet, the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is prized by the world; when encountered by such people, it instead turns into poison.
Even if one’s talent rivals that of Aśvaghoṣa and one’s understanding equals that of Nāgārjuna, one will only have one or two more lifetimes before losing the human form. At the point of death...

At the time of death, if even a single hair’s breadth of the mental capacity of sage or ordinary being is not exhausted, or if even a speck of dust of thought has not been forgotten, one will be reborn according to those thoughts.
With the five aggregates, heavy or light, one will take form within the wombs of donkeys or horses, or be boiled and roasted amidst cauldrons of boiling water and furnace coals.

The previous mindfulness, recollection, insights, and understandings were all lost at once; returning to their former state, they became ants once more, and from the beginning again became mosquitoes and gadflies.
Though these were virtuous causes, they brought about evil fruits.

"Attaining the meaning and forgetting the words. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Ordinary people and fools do not understand their own nature; they do not recognize the true Buddha within their own bodies. They long for the West while facing the East, or long for the East while facing the West.
Master Zhi said: "The wise know that the mind is the Buddha; the ignorant love to go to the West. This is because the Dharma...
There is concealment and manifestation; the teachings have provisional and ultimate aspects; human faculties are either sharp or dull; and the Patriarchs employ suppression or encouragement.
This is like how illnesses differ and prescriptions vary accordingly. Suppose someone suffers from a fever that has caused delirium; one must treat it with a cold medicine.
If, upon hearing that the cold medicine is effective, one were to declare that cinnamon and ginger are useless, would this not be a great error? The Sixth Patriarch transmitted the Mind alone.

Master Yin was precisely one who praised the Mahāyāna, pointing directly to the human mind so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha. In this, both the Buddha and the Dharma are transcended, and no reliance is placed on words and letters.
How could he have taught people to recite the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth? It is simply that when one grasps the meaning and forgets the words, they are harmonized;
once there is thorough understanding, there is naturally no contradiction.
Regarding the body, gain and loss, and the rites of gods and men, the verse on the dry bone says: "You were my former life; today my celestial eye has opened. Precious robes arrive upon thought;
jade-like food comes spontaneously. I thank you for your past diligent toil, which has made me feel such joy today. [This was spoken] at the time of scattering flowers.
Prostrate twice. Let no one in the human world be startled or suspicious. Furthermore, the verse on the hungry ghosts whipping corpses says:

"Because of this stinking skin-sack, one is busily frantic from kalpa to kalpa; knowing only how to crave pleasure, one refuses to turn the light back for even a moment. Meritorious deeds are as few as a grain of sesame."
The years in the Yellow Springs are long; one must strike with a severe staff. This resentment is suddenly difficult to forget.
If these words were used to transform the common people, they could be considered sincere. Yet, this is not possible. Why? Because humans and spirits are entrusted within the physical frame.
That which employs the physical frame is entirely the spirit. Therefore, those who are celestial beings are those who, in their previous lives, made excellent use of the physical frame.

Those who become hungry ghosts were those who, in their previous lives, did not make proper use of their physical bodies. Whether they attained success or met with failure rested entirely upon that moment;
yet once they have received their retribution, what benefit is there in honoring them or whipping them?
The *Dvayadevaputra-sūtra* states: "When a person is born, two devaputras follow them: the first is called 'Co-born' (*sahaja*), and the second is called 'Same-name' (*samānanāman*).
These devaputras always see the person, but the person does not see the devaputras. Are these two devaputras not the youths of the two classes—the virtuous and the non-virtuous?"
Are you not among their followers? When a person raises an intention, utters a word, or takes a step, they should constantly reflect: "Will these two heavenly beings see me and feel no shame?
If one cultivates the Pure Land in this manner, one will certainly attain rebirth in the highest grade.
Among minor causes, there is the person who builds a bridge and the person who destroys a bridge; these are minor causes for heaven and hell.

There is the person who rides in a palanquin and the person who carries the palanquin; these are minor effects of heaven and hell. One may extend this principle to all similar categories; it is universally applicable.
It is seen. Constantly examine the mind in this manner to cultivate the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land.

As a lay bodhisattva who provides for his livelihood while assisting the Path, he belongs to the eminent ranks of those who practice Buddha-recitation. Daily he attends the vegetarian feasts of donors, sitting and enjoying the offerings of humans and devas.
All these are not the true path. It is better to manage one's livelihood; if one has the intention to practice, how could it hinder one’s labors?

Whether tilling the fields and sowing seeds, or conducting business in the marketplace, whether possessing abundant family wealth or seeking a mere pint or two daily—one should reflect that diligence prevents idleness and frugality leads to surplus.
To cultivate oneself in this way is to be a true child of the Buddha. If, however, one is extravagant and indolent, [one is no such child].

When one's livelihood is desolate, although one wishes to practice the Way, it cannot be accomplished. One should know with certainty that worldly governance and the means of livelihood all accord with the True Dharma;
crafts and technical skills benefit all living beings. If one desires to cultivate pure karma, one should employ these means of livelihood to assist the Path.
All sentient beings suffer; having not yet awakened to perfect enlightenment, they dwell within a great dream, ascending and descending through the six realms of existence without ever ceasing.

Though the gods possess joy, their retribution eventually exhausts and their signs of prosperity decline. When the asuras are filled with rage, they wage war against one another, each seeking victory. As for the animals—whether flying or running—[they endure their own hardships].
Devouring one another and preying upon each other; the dark and hidden realms of ghosts and spirits, where they are oppressed by hunger and thirst;

and the long night of hell, with its agonizing cries—having attained birth in the human realm is surely to be considered a blessing. Yet, even there, one is entangled by the manifold sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Only this Pure Land is free from all such suffering.

The quiescence and function are unimpeded, blazing forth in activity while remaining unmoved from the fundamental limit (*mūla-koṭi*). It is like water giving rise to waves; the waves are entirely water. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says:

To depart from delusion is itself the truth;

the true self is inherently present, yet through delusion it seems non-existent, like the moon obscured by clouds. The false self is inherently non-existent, yet through grasping it appears to exist, like a flower reflected in a mirror.
One must know that the mind is itself without marks, arising only by relying on objects; its nature is fundamentally empty, yet it functions through the mind.
Thus it manifests. If one wishes to leave delusion behind and attain the truth, one must single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

Deluded ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas; afflictions are themselves Bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha.
The preceding thought that clings to objects is affliction; the subsequent thought that detaches from objects is bodhi.
Thus we know that Amitābha and sentient beings are separated by nothing more than the shift of a single thought-moment.
There is nothing that is not Buddha;

Sentient beings throughout the six realms are fundamentally Buddha, yet due to delusion and ignorance, they are unwilling to recite the Buddha’s name. When the wise attain awakening, they see their nature and become Buddhas.
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni revealed the practice of *nien-fo*; Amitābha has vows to receive and guide those who practice *nien-fo*;

The Buddhas of the six directions collectively praise the mindfulness of the Buddha. The Patriarchs established the teachings and exhorted people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Among all shortcut Dharma-gates, there is only the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Every single one of the successive generations of Patriarchs practiced mindfulness of the Buddha; every person among the famous worthies of past and present practiced mindfulness of the Buddha.
I now possess the karmic affinity to encounter the mindfulness of the Buddha. Mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the mind; mindfulness of the mind, mindfulness of the Buddha.

My mouth constantly recites the name of the Buddha; my mind constantly reveres the Buddha; my eyes constantly contemplate the Buddha; my ears constantly listen to the Buddha; my body constantly prostrates to the Buddha; and my nose constantly perceives the fragrance of the Buddha.
With incense, flowers, lamps, and candles, one constantly makes offerings to the Buddha. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one is never separated from the Buddha.

Amidst suffering or joy, adversity or favor, one does not forget to mindfully recollect the Buddha. In putting on clothes or eating food, there is nothing that is not the Buddha. In every place and at every moment, all things are entirely the Buddha.
Movement is the Buddha; stillness is the Buddha. Busyness is the Buddha; leisure is the Buddha. Horizontality is the Buddha;
verticality is the Buddha. Goodness is the Buddha; evil is the Buddha. Birth is the Buddha; death is the Buddha.

Every thought-moment is the Buddha; every mind is the Buddha. When impermanence arrives, this is precisely the time to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Letting go of all attachments, one proceeds directly home to behold the Buddha.
A single sphere of perfect radiance is the Buddha of the emptiness of nature. To realize this single thought is what is called being a Buddha.

It is eternally abiding and indestructible. The Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body Buddhas of Amitāyus are of one and the same essence. The thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas are all one and the same Buddha.
I universally exhort those with the karmic affinity to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. If you do not recite the Buddha’s name, you will lose the Original Buddha.

Greed, anger, and jealousy cause one to lose the Buddha within oneself. Alcohol, lust, wealth, and arrogance defile the true, celestial Buddha. The six thieves—self-importance, ego, right, and wrong—plunder the Buddha.
When the single breath no longer returns, where can one seek the Buddha? In the hells and the three miserable realms, one shall never again hear the name of the Buddha.
Throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one may regret not having practiced mindfulness of the Buddha. I urge you earnestly: practice mindfulness of the Buddha within yourself.
Swiftly turn the light back upon its source; do not seek the Buddha elsewhere. If every thought is clear and undeluded, who is not a Buddha? May all people take refuge in the Buddha themselves.
Dedicate the merit toward the Western Pure Land and make vows to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. At the time of death, one will behold the Buddha through mindfulness;
upon the lotus throne of the nine grades, one will pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and attain the unobstructed eye, seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions.

In the *Qingzhu ji* (Collection on the Pure Pearl), an ancient master said: "When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the water cannot fail to become clear.
